prompt: Tell me a story in five sentences about a girl and her dog.
generations: Junie was seven when Maple's muzzle first went gray, and eleven when the old collie stopped waking at the sound of her bike in the driveway. That last autumn Junie carried her down the porch steps each morning so she could smell the cold air and pretend to hunt squirrels. On a Tuesday in November Maple refused her food, and the vet said gently that there was nothing left to fix, only comfort left to give. She died two days later with her head in Junie's lap, in the sun patch by the kitchen door where she had always slept, and Junie did not let go for a long while. That spring, Junie planted a red maple over the grave by the fence line, and every October since she has stood under it and said out loud that the leaves are exactly the right color.

On the last morning at the farmhouse, the movers propped both doors open, and Nell's brown mutt Barnaby slipped past their boots and vanished into the tall corn. The family searched until the flashlights dimmed, then drove three hundred miles to the city apartment with an empty crate rattling in the trunk. Nell taped flyers to bus shelters, woke certain she had heard him barking in the stairwell, and would not let her mother give away his blanket. In late October a farmer two counties over called about a thin dog who kept sleeping on the porch of an empty white house and growled at anyone who tried to move him. Nell was out of the car before it stopped rolling, and Barnaby came down those steps as though the eleven weeks between them had never happened at all.

The first time thunder cracked over the hill, Priya's beagle lifted his head and said, quite calmly, that she ought to bring the wash in. After that she learned the rule: Dodger could speak only while a storm stood directly overhead, and only ever to her. One August night, with the windows shuddering in their frames, he told her why he had turned up at their door six years earlier — her grandmother had asked him, on her last morning, to stay until Priya was grown. He warned her that she must never repeat it, because a promise spoken aloud in dry weather comes undone. So she keeps it: on clear days she scratches his ears and says nothing at all, and on stormy nights they talk until the thunder rolls east.

This morning they strapped a stiff blue bag onto my girl's back, and she smelled sharp and nervous, the way she does when the vacuum comes out. I walked her to the corner with my shoulder against her knee, and then a long yellow machine swallowed her up and drove off with my whole heart inside it. The house went wrong after that: no crumbs, no sock game, no small hand on my ribs, only the terrible ticking clock and Mother telling me to lie down. I lay in the hallway with my chin on her left shoe, guarding it, because a dog keeps what he can keep. Then the door banged and she was back, taller somehow and smelling of glue and strange children, and she knelt down and told me everything, and I understood every word.

Ship's clock read year fourteen of the crossing when the breach alarm pulled Tam out of her cot; of nine hundred souls aboard the colony ship *Verity*, only she and Rook were awake. Rook had been engineered for vacuum work — thumbed forepaws, sealed sinuses that read pressure the way other dogs read smells — and he was already at the corridor hatch, growling low at Section C. He led her through the dark to the crack, a hairline seam weeping frost from a micrometeorite strike, and he stood braced against the suction while she pumped sealant into it with numb fingers. When the wind died and the gauges climbed back to green, Tam sat down hard on the deck plating and let him press his whole heavy head into her chest. Eight hundred ninety-eight sleepers never knew, and Tam decided that was fine, because Rook already knew, and he was the only one whose opinion she needed.

Odessa heard the man before she felt him — "let me get you across, sweetheart" — and then his hand closed on Sable's harness and hauled them both off the curb. Sable did not fight the stranger; she simply locked her legs and threw her weight backward against Odessa's thigh, the signal that meant *stop, wrong, danger*, and Odessa stopped. A delivery truck went by close enough to snap the hem of her coat, and the man's grip fell away with an apology he hadn't finished thinking of. Odessa found the harness handle, told him quietly that grabbing a working dog could get its person killed, and then said, "Sable, forward," and the crossing happened exactly as it always did. On the far corner she crouched and pressed her forehead to the dog's, and Sable's tail beat twice against the pavement, and that was all either of them needed to say about it.

By the spring of 1935 the wheat in Cimarron County had blown away to Kansas, and supper at the Ledbetter place depended on Ruthie and a wire-haired terrier named Scrap. They hunted the dry washes at dawn while the air was still clean, Ruthie with her brother's slingshot and Scrap running the jackrabbits out of the sagebrush in tight, furious circles. He was eighteen pounds of ribs and stubbornness, and he never once ate before the family did, though Ruthie always saved him the liver. On the day the black duster came rolling in like a mountain laid on its side, Scrap drove a rabbit straight to her feet and then dragged her by the skirt hem toward the cellar door. That night they ate stew with grit in it by lamplight, and Ruthie fed him from her own bowl and told him he was the best hand her daddy ever had.

At the county shelter every family crowded around the pen of fat golden puppies, so nobody looked at the last kennel, where a middle-aged mutt with one folded ear and a gray chin lay facing the wall. Marguerite, who had moved to town in January and still ate lunch alone, sat down on the concrete outside his gate and waited without saying anything. It took twenty minutes for him to turn around, and another ten before he came close enough to breathe on her knuckles through the wire. The volunteer said he'd been there eleven months and had a bad hip and no name anybody knew, and Marguerite said that was all right, because she'd been nobody's first choice either. She called him Wednesday, and on the drive home he put his gray chin on her forearm and left it there the whole way, and neither of them was lonely after that.

The creek behind the Hollisters' barn had been a trickle all August, but three days of rain turned it into something with a will of its own, and Cora went in after her hat. The water took her legs, then her breath, and slammed her against a snag of fence wire twenty yards downstream, and the last thing she heard clearly was Duke's furious barking above her. He came off the bank flat out, got her sleeve in his teeth, and hauled — a black-and-white farm collie against a flooded creek — dragging her into the shallows before the current swung them both under. Her father found them there at dusk, and the vet worked past midnight, then straightened up and said the ribs were cracked and one paw was torn to the pad but the dog would run again by winter. Cora leaned over the table, put her lips against Duke's wet ear, and whispered thank you, thank you, thank you until he thumped his tail.

Marisol's science fair project was fourteen slices of bread in labeled trays, each one growing a different beautiful and disgusting mold. The night before the fair, Barkley the corgi nosed the basement door open and ate thirteen of them, leaving only the tray of blue-green *Penicillium* untouched and, insultingly, licked clean around the edges. Marisol cried for eleven minutes, then stayed up until one in the morning rebuilding her poster around the question of why a dog who eats garbage would refuse exactly one mold. The judges spent a long time at her table, asked three questions about antifungal compounds and canine scent aversion, and awarded her the blue ribbon in Life Sciences. Barkley got no credit, which was fine with him, because he had already been paid in bread.

prompt: Tell me a story in five sentences about a boy and his dog.
generations: Caleb found the pup shivering under the corn crib the spring he turned nine, and though his father said the farm had no room for another mouth, the boy shared his supper anyway and named him Boone. All that summer they worked the fields together, the shaggy brown dog trotting at the heels of the boy who taught him to fetch, sit, and wait at the edge of the road. When the March thaw swelled the creek and the ice gave way beneath Caleb's boots, it was Boone who plunged into the brown water, clamped his jaws on the boy's collar, and hauled him thrashing to the willow roots on the bank. Caleb never told anyone how long he lay there in the mud with his arms around the dog's soaked neck, but afterward he never went to the creek without him. They grew gray together over fourteen seasons, the man and the old dog, and when Boone finally slept in the sun for the last time, Caleb buried him under the willow where the water had given them both back.

Sam was six when Rusty came home in a cardboard box, and he was seventeen when the old dog could no longer climb the porch steps without help. That last winter, Sam carried him outside every morning to smell the cold air, and Rusty would thump his tail twice, which was all the thanks he had left to give. The morning it happened, Sam sat on the kitchen floor with his hand on the dog's ribs and felt the breathing get shallow and then stop, and he did not cry until his mother touched his shoulder. For weeks the house was unbearably quiet in all the places Rusty used to be — the rug by the heater, the spot beneath the table where crumbs fell. Then one evening Sam caught himself smiling at nothing, remembering the ridiculous way Rusty used to sneeze when he was happy, and he understood that grief was not a room he was trapped in but a thing he would carry, and that carrying it was the last kindness he could do for his friend.

The storm came off the ridge faster than the forecast promised, and by four o'clock nobody in Hollis Fork could find eleven-year-old Danny Pryor. Half the town gathered at the fire hall with flashlights and thermoses while the snow erased every track in the fields, and the search captain admitted they were guessing. It was Danny's mutt, Pepper, who would not stop barking at the back door — and when they finally let her out, she went straight past the road and up the fence line into the dark. The men followed her for a mile and a half through drifts to her waist, cursing and stumbling, until she stopped at a collapsed hay shelter and dug frantically at the snow packed against its leeward side. They pulled the boy out blue-lipped but breathing, and every winter since, when the first flakes fall, Danny still says the dog he was supposed to protect is the reason he grew up at all.

I did not know his name at first; he was just the small loud thing that smelled of milk and grass, and I decided that he was mine. I learned the sound of his bicycle from three streets away, and I learned that when he came home crying from the school bus he needed me to put my head in his lap and stay very still. I guarded his window in the summer, ate the vegetables he hid under the table, and slept across his door so nothing could get in without stepping over me. Somewhere in there he got tall and his voice went low and he started smelling of soap and other people, but he still said my name the same way. Now his hand is on my ribs and his face is wet, and I am so tired, but I am wagging, because I want him to know I would do all of it again.

At last he stopped crying and said the dog had lived a good long life, and his father agreed. That was the same year the gray-muzzled dog could no longer manage the stairs, and the boy carried her up every night. Before that came all the ordinary years — the ball games, the sledding, the summers when she swam out after every stick he threw. Earlier still, she was a leggy pup who chewed his sneakers to ribbons and was forgiven each time. And earliest of all, there was a rainy Saturday, a cardboard box outside the feed store, and a boy kneeling down as one small wet nose pushed itself into his open hand.

In the spring of 1943, Tommy Hale mailed the form to Dogs for Defense and then walked his shepherd, Ranger, to the train station himself, because he had promised not to cry and a promise is a promise. The letters came back from the Quartermaster Corps in careful typed lines: Ranger had been trained as a sentry, Ranger had shipped to the Pacific, Ranger was performing his duty well. Tommy kept the letters in a cigar box and marked the war map on his bedroom wall with pins he could not really justify. In November 1945 a truck stopped at the end of the lane and a soldier led down a dog who was thinner, grayer at the muzzle, and who flinched at the sound of the screen door. Tommy sat down in the gravel and waited, saying nothing at all, until at last Ranger crossed the last ten feet and pressed his head against the boy's chest the way he always had.

June 9 — Uncle Ray brought a black pup with one white ear and said I could keep him if I did the feeding, so his name is Domino and I did the feeding. July 2 — Domino swam in the reservoir today even though he had clearly never swum before, and I had to go in after him, and Mom says my sneakers are a lost cause. July 21 — I told Domino about Dad's new apartment and he just put his chin on my foot and stayed there for about an hour, which is more than anybody else did. August 14 — He got out through the gate and I looked for him until dark, and when I found him asleep on the porch I yelled at him and then hugged him and then yelled at him again. August 31 — School tomorrow, and I want to write down that this was the best summer I ever had, in case I need to remember later exactly why.

In a village at the edge of the black forest there lived a woodcutter's son named Jorin, who owned nothing but an axe too heavy for him and a great shaggy hound that had followed him home out of the snow. The villagers said the beast was ill-omened, for no dog had eyes the color of amber lantern-glass, but Jorin only scratched its ears and shared his black bread. One winter night the wolves came down from the ridge, and the hound rose up between the boy and the door, and where its shadow fell upon the wall it was not the shadow of a dog but of a tall crowned figure with a spear. By morning the snow was unmarked, the wolves were gone, and the hound slept by the coals as though it had never stirred. Jorin grew to be a woodcutter with sons of his own, and he never once asked the creature what it truly was, for he had learned that some gifts are kept only by leaving them unopened.

Eleven-year-old Piotr had never seen a real dog, only the archives, but his companion unit ARLO walked and wagged and warmed his feet through the long night-cycles of the generation ship *Verity*. In the ship's one-hundred-and-fourth year, ARLO began to stutter — forgetting the way to the hydroponics deck, calling Piotr by the name of a boy four generations dead. The maintenance chief said the memory lattice was degrading and the fabricators could no longer produce the alloy to repair it, and offered to wipe and reinitialize the unit as a fresh companion. Piotr refused, and instead spent his evenings reading their shared logs aloud, teaching ARLO the same walk to hydroponics again and again as the dog's failing mind lost it again and again. When the *Verity* finally reached orbit around the green world, Piotr, gray-haired now, carried the silent chassis down to the grass so that whatever was left of it could rest under a real sky.

It began, as these things do, with a genuine incident: Marcus's dog Waffles ate three pages of his social studies report, and Marcus decided that the truth was simply too embarrassing to survive fifth grade. So he told Mr. Delgado his printer had exploded, which required a story about the smoke, which required a story about the fire department, which by Thursday had grown into a small neighborhood evacuation and a commendation from the mayor. The trouble was that Mr. Delgado, moved by the boy's ordeal, arranged an assembly to honor Marcus's bravery, complete with a certificate and Marcus's mother in the second row wearing an expression of pure, dawning confusion. Standing at the microphone before four hundred people, Marcus looked at the certificate, looked at his mother, and heard himself say, "My dog ate my homework." There was a very long silence, and then Mr. Delgado said, "You know, Marcus, that's the first thing you've told me all week that I actually believe."

prompt: Tell me the plot line in 5 sentences for a romcom movie set in rural Kansas for Easter.
generations: Burned-out Kansas City ad executive Delia Mercer inherits her late grandmother's foundering egg farm outside Pratt, Kansas, along with three thousand hens, a leaking henhouse roof, and forty-one days until the Easter rush that could pay off the bank note. Her only hope is Wes Bogard, the stubborn local handyman who still hasn't forgiven her for leaving him standing under a paper-streamer arch at senior prom before she fled for the city. As they repaint nesting boxes and pitch "heritage rainbow eggs" to church committees and grocers, their bickering thaws into the easy rhythm they had at seventeen, and Delia starts sleeping through the night for the first time in years. Then her old agency offers her a partnership contingent on selling the land to a developer, and Wes finds the contract on the kitchen table the night before the farm's big Easter market debut. Delia torches the deal in the burn barrel, and on Easter morning she and Wes hand out dyed eggs to half the county from a truck bed, finally getting the kiss the prom never gave them.

Stranded by a dead alternator on a gravel road in Barber County, drifting session guitarist Cal Ruiz accepts a ride from Junie Yoder, who is driving home for Easter dreading her grandmother's annual interrogation about her love life. Panicked at the mailbox, Junie introduces Cal as her fiance, and her matchmaking Baptist grandmother immediately installs him in the guest room, puts him on the sunrise-service program, and starts negotiating a June wedding date. Cal proves alarmingly good at the role, charming the aunts, memorizing hymns, and dyeing eggs with Junie's nieces, while Junie's rehearsed lies keep colliding with how much she actually likes him. The engagement unravels at Easter dinner when Cal's real ex-girlfriend calls the landline and Grandma answers, and the whole ham-and-deviled-egg table learns the truth at once. Junie chases Cal to the bus stop in Medicine Lodge and offers him something better than a fake ring: a real first date, starting with breakfast.

Documentary filmmaker Priya Nair drives into Rooks County the Thursday before Easter to shoot footage of vanishing family wheat farms, and gets exactly one interview before a tornado siren sends her sprinting into Dell Hoyt's storm cellar with her camera still rolling. Dell, a laconic fourth-generation farmer, says roughly eleven words in the first six hours; Priya, who fills silence for a living, talks enough for both of them. With the road washed out and the power gone until Sunday, they share jars of pickled beets, a battery radio, and increasingly honest confessions about the ambitions and losses that keep each of them alone. By Saturday night Priya has stopped filming and started listening, and Dell has started talking, and both realize that whatever this is, it won't survive her flight back east. Easter morning they climb out into a rinsed-clean sky and walk to the little church on the section line, where Dell finally asks her to stay for the summer harvest — and she asks him to be in her film instead of just behind it.

Large-animal veterinarian Nora Kettering is called out to the Whitlow sheep ranch near Elk Falls during Holy Week, where a botched vaccination schedule and a bad batch of feed have turned lambing season into a full-blown crisis. Waiting for her is Beckett Whitlow, the ranch's cynical heir, who flew in from Denver to sign the land over to a wind-lease broker and considers every rescued lamb an argument he's already lost. Working shoulder-deep in the lambing barn through freezing nights, they trade insults, then histories, then a kiss beside a heat lamp at three in the morning after saving a set of triplets. Nora convinces Beckett to bring the orphan bottle-lambs to the town's Easter egg hunt, where the sight of local kids feeding them cracks something open in him. On Easter Sunday he tears up the broker's paperwork, offers Nora a partnership in a new veterinary practice on the ranch, and admits he never wanted to leave, only to be asked to stay.

Twenty years after their breakup on the courthouse lawn, Maren Kirby and Sam Delacroix are named co-grand-marshals of Fairhaven, Kansas's centennial Easter parade, a decision the committee makes purely because their families donated the biggest floats. Maren, back in town running her father's hardware store after a divorce, wants to ride in separate convertibles; Sam, the widowed high school band director, wants to finally know why she stopped writing. Six weeks of planning meetings, egg-hunt logistics, and one disastrous joint appearance on the local radio show force them to share a truck cab, an argument they never finished, and a bag of jellybeans. When the centennial time capsule is opened, it holds Maren's unsent 1999 letter explaining everything, read aloud by a mortified fourth-grader at the pre-parade assembly. On Easter Sunday they ride the same float down Main Street under a banner reading ONE HUNDRED YEARS OF BEGINNINGS, holding hands where the whole town can see.

When the pastors of Hesper Community Church and Bethel Lutheran can't agree on a joint Easter egg hunt, the two congregations schedule rival hunts for the same hour on the same Saturday, three miles apart in the same Kansas township. Lead planners Tessa Dahlgren and Owen Prentice — competitive since 4-H — escalate from dueling flyers to a helicopter candy drop and a rumored petting zoo, until the county fairgrounds double-books them into a single shared field. Forced to co-plan from one cramped grange hall office with one working printer, they discover their spreadsheets are compatible, their arguments are fun, and their coffee orders are identical. A prank war ends with eight thousand plastic eggs spilled across the highway and the two of them sorting candy on a tailgate at midnight, laughing too hard to keep score. The merged hunt is the biggest in county history, and on Easter morning Tessa hides one golden egg with Owen's name on it, containing an invitation to dinner and an admission that she'd rather partner than beat him.

Serial dater Georgia Pruitt, whose romantic track record is the most reliable entertainment in Sedgwick County, gives up men for Lent as a joke she fully intends to keep, and forty minutes later meets soil scientist Elias Vance in the ash-smudged crowd outside St. Bede's. He is, unfortunately, perfect: patient, funny, tall enough, and renting the guest cottage on her family's farm for the entire forty days. Georgia dodges him with increasingly baroque strategies — installing herself as choir accompanist, taking up early-morning fence repair, volunteering for every church supper in the parish — while Elias cheerfully assumes she simply hates him. Her best friend keeps a chalkboard tally of days remaining, her mother keeps inviting him to dinner, and Georgia keeps discovering that avoiding someone is its own kind of falling. On Holy Saturday, Elias announces his contract ended early and he's leaving before sunrise, so Georgia drives to the cottage at 11:52 p.m., waits eight minutes on the porch step, and then knocks.

Ten-year-old twins Ruthie and Cal Simms decide their widowed dad, Mack, has been alone long enough, and pick as his match Dr. Ivy Bergstrom, the widowed pharmacist whose daughter Pia joins the conspiracy at recess. The three kids volunteer to hide eggs for the annual hunt at the Little Arkansas River park, then rig the entire course: numbered clue-eggs that lead the adults away from the children and toward each other through a windbreak, a footbridge, and a picnic table set with two folding chairs. The plan mostly works — Mack and Ivy meet at the table, awkward and suspicious, and share a thermos of coffee and a conversation about grief that neither has managed with anyone else. It also nearly collapses when the kids' scheming gets them banned from the hunt and Ivy accuses Mack of orchestrating it, sending him home humiliated and both parents retreating into their old careful loneliness. On Easter morning the children stage one last, terrible, entirely transparent trick: a single golden egg on the church steps containing two words, ASK HER, which Mack finally does.

Fifth-generation ham farmer Boone Halloran and vegan bakery owner Simone Achebe have publicly loathed each other since her billboard about "kindness on your plate" went up across the highway from his smokehouse in Chase County. When the centennial Easter Community Banquet's caterer breaks an ankle, the mayor hires them both, splitting the menu down the middle and seating them at the same prep table in the school cafeteria for two weeks. Their sabotage — mislabeled pans, a stolen glaze recipe, an unauthorized aquafaba meringue on his signature pie — gradually becomes collaboration as each admits the other's food is infuriatingly good. Late one night, tasting each other's dishes with the lights off so nobody in town sees, they find a common language in cardamom, sorghum, and the grandmothers who taught them both to cook. The banquet is a triumph of two tables that keep getting mixed up, and on Easter Sunday they announce a shared storefront on Main Street, with a wall down the middle and a door in it.

Two towns twelve miles apart in Reno County, Kansas, both lose their Easter Bunny performers the same week, so the temp agency sends Marisol Quintana to the Hutchinson mall and Theo Brand to the county fairgrounds egg hunt — with one shared costume they must trade in the parking lot of a Dairy Barn every afternoon. Bound by the agency's strict no-unmasking rule and a mutually terrible sense of timing, they get to know each other entirely through the notes, snacks, and increasingly flirtatious cassette tapes they leave zipped in the costume's head. Over three weeks of handoffs, they trade childhood stories and confessions neither has said aloud, falling for a voice, a handwriting, and a pair of ears. Complications multiply: Marisol assumes he's the surly mascot who once scolded her about pinning, and Theo believes she's an out-of-towner who leaves in April. They agree to finally meet unmasked at sunrise Easter morning at the fairgrounds gate, where they discover they've already met — badly, twice — and that the third time is the one that counts.

prompt: Write a haiku about a whale and a walnut tree.
generations:
green swell of walnut
leaves — a whale rolls through the wind
and sounds for the sky

under walnut roots
a rib cage curves — this dry hill
remembers its sea

one walnut shell holds
the whole ocean; the whale swims
around the world-tree

walnuts thud all night
the last whale passes southward —
both bound for winter

walnut plank adrift
a barnacled flank rises,
whale nudges it home

in walnut he carves
a whale rising from the bench —
shavings, then the sea

cracked walnut, two lobes:
a small brain in my palm — his
fills the whole ocean

churchyard walnut tree
shades the names lost to the bay —
spout offshore, then rain

rope swing, walnut shade
he kicks off — a chalk whale breaks
the driveway's blue sea

a whale, forty tons
one walnut tree on the hill
both still in gray light

prompt: Write a short love poem with 4 lines.
generations:
The moon lays silver on the restless sea,
and roses lean to catch the falling light;
so all my wandering hours return to thee
as tides return to shore each windless night.

We are two curves that lean toward one same line,
halving the distance, halving it again;
no final contact comes—and still you're mine:
love is the limit math can't quite explain.

You warm the cup before you pour the tea;
you fold my shirts in halves I never learned.
Devotion is the porch light left for me,
still burning at whatever hour I've returned.

Your hands are maps now, rivered blue and thin,
that once wrote letters I could not put down.
I trace the girl still living in your skin
and kiss the sixty winters in your crown.

They promised time would take you, bit by bit;
it hasn't. Still I leave the hallway light,
still keep your side untouched, still cannot quit
reaching for the impossible each night.

He doesn't know. I keep it like a stone
warmed in my pocket, smooth from being turned.
I say his name to lamplight, all alone—
the only witness to how long I've burned.

We learned in whispers first, then learned in light:
two women, burnt toast, laughter, Sunday rain.
Our hands stayed joined the whole way home last night—
the street said nothing. Nothing to explain.

Long after every lamp in town goes dark,
Only your breathing keeps my hours in time.
Voices may fade, and summers lose their spark—
Even then, you remain my only rhyme.

You wait beside the door as though for war,
though I was only out to fetch the bread.
Grey-muzzled, thumping, glad—and nothing more
is asked of me. Good dog. Come. Rest your head.

Body, I hurried you for thirty years,
faulted your softness, blamed your crooked start.
Tonight I meet your eyes, and past the tears
I say: you carried me. Come here, sweetheart.

prompt: Write a short poem of hatred with 4 lines.
generations:
I loved you once; the word still tastes of rust.
You made a stranger of the mouth I knew.
Now every tenderness I ever gave
turns in me like a key that locks out you.

The mirror keeps a face I cannot pardon;
each morning it returns what I have made.
I hate the coward's mouth, the borrowed courage,
the hands that folded every time they prayed.

I hated you the way a house holds smoke—
each room of me grew darker, breath by breath.
Today I opened windows, said your name,
and let it out. I want my air, not death.

Hate came as damp, one droplet on a hinge,
a small brown blossom nobody wiped clean.
It ate the door, the frame, the standing house—
now wind walks through the lace where I had been.

I am the sea, and I have counted you:
your hulls, your hymns, your names cut into stone.
I hate the salt you borrowed from my mouth.
I am coming, slowly, for my own.

My grandfather bequeathed me half a field,
a rifle, and the surname we don't say.
I've never met the man beyond the wall—
I hate him fluently. It's how we pray.

I hate the cruelty that dresses well,
that signs the order with a steady hand,
that calls the hungry idle, calls the drowned
a policy. I hate it where I stand.

Ten thousand times your palm, and never kind:
you shove me, kick me, curse the way I stick.
I've swallowed every quarrel in this house—
some night I'll swell against the frame and hold.

I am Hate. I was born the hour you turned away,
small as a splinter, patient as a stone.
I need no feeding; you rehearse me nightly.
Bolt every door. I'm already home.

I hate the clock that screams me from my bed,
I hate the brake lights blooming red on red,
I hate the Monday grinning at the gate—
I'd skip all three, but naturally, I'm late.

prompt: Write a short fable about a lemur and a light bulb.
generations:
A ring-tailed lemur, the vainest of his troop, sunned himself each dawn on the highest rock so that all might admire the thirteen perfect bands of his tail. One night a light appeared below in the researchers' camp: a small white fire caged in a glass fruit, hung from a pole.

"The moon has been captured," he said, "and left there for the taking. Let me wear the moon, and I shall be admired at midnight as well as at noon."

Down he crept, up the pole he climbed, and with both hands he seized the glass. The heat went through his palms like a hundred wasps. He fell howling into the dust, and the camp dogs chased him back into the thorny dark.

For a week he could not open his hands to groom himself, and the troop groomed around him — in pity, not in awe. At last he climbed his rock again, palms wrapped in leaves, and let the true sun warm them: a light that cost him nothing, and that he had never once thought to thank.

Moral: Light you have not earned lends no glory; it only leaves its mark upon your hands.

High in a village mango tree, a light bulb was strung up to keep thieves away, and it took itself for a small sun.

"Look at me," it told the lemur who came each night for fruit. "I make my own day. You poor creature, you must sit in the dark half your life, waiting for a sun you do not own. I never wait. I never sleep. I am brilliance without pause."

"That is a great deal of brilliance," said the lemur, and went on eating.

"You could stay and be lit by me," the bulb said. "Under my glow you would almost be somebody."

"I am somebody in the dark," said the lemur, and curled into the fork of a branch with her tail over her nose.

The bulb blazed on, insulted, all through the small hours. Somewhere near the fourth hour it made a soft sound, like a seed cracking, and went black, and its filament lay broken as a hair.

The lemur did not stir. She had nothing to say about it, and no lesson to draw. She simply slept until the grey came up over the hills, opened her eyes, spread her white belly to the east, and was warm.

Moral: none was offered. The bulb had made all the speeches, and the dawn arrived anyway.

I remember the moment I began. A shudder came up the wire, my filament drew tight and white, and I hung in the doorway of the veranda saying HERE, HERE, HERE to a hillside that had never asked.

On my ninth night she came: a lemur with a black-and-white tail, sitting on the rail just beyond my reach, staring at me with two round mirrors for eyes. She came every night after. She never touched me. She would look, and eat a fig, and look again, and go.

I thought at first she loved me. Then I saw the moths.

They came for me by the hundred, drunk and blundering, and she picked them off the air as easily as fruit. I was her lantern; I was her lure. Every hour I burned made her supper. I confess I was ashamed, and then I was not: what else is a light for, if not to gather the living around it?

The seasons went. She grew slower. She brought a small one with a crooked ear who learned the rail. My glass went dim with dust and the ghosts of wings.

Now I feel the thinness in me, the place where my filament has worn to nearly nothing. She is on the rail. She is looking. There is a taste of breaking, and —

Moral: I was never the light. I was only the narrow place the light passed through, and while it passed, something out there was fed.

In the first days, the lemurs were creatures of the afternoon. Their eyes were small and brown and modest, and they slept from dusk to dawn like sensible people.

Then strangers came ashore and raised a house of tin, and in its window they hung a bulb, and at nightfall the bulb woke.

Old Vola, greatest-grandmother of every lemur since, crossed the river to see it. "This is a star that has agreed to stay still," she said, and she sat on the fence post and looked at it. She looked all night. She looked the next night, and the next, and for thirty nights, until the shape of it was printed on the inside of her head and she could not blink it away. When at last she turned back to the forest, the forest was only a wall of black. She had traded her darkness for a lamp that was not hers, and now she could not see her own hands.

She wept at the foot of a tamarind, and the forest, which does not forgive but does repay, laid two thin sheets of moonlight behind her eyes — mirrors, to catch whatever little light remained and use it twice.

So Vola saw again, but only at night, and only in silver, and her children after her.

That is why the lemur's eyes are huge, and why they flash back at you when you swing your torch through the branches. The forest paid her debt. It did not undo her mistake.

Moral: What you stare at too long, you will carry behind your eyes forever; be careful what you make of your looking.

At the edge of a cleared field a lemur found a glass fruit lying in the grass — round, cold, with a curl of black thread inside and a strange metal stem.

"I have seen these hanging in the settlement," she said. "They hold a piece of the day. This one has fallen asleep."

So she set about waking it. She warmed it under her arms all afternoon; it stayed cold. She rubbed it with dry leaves until her palms stung; nothing. She soaked it in dew, laid it in the path of the noon sun, buried it three days in the black soil where seeds are taught to wake. She caught nine fireflies and held them against the glass, hoping the light might be persuaded to move house. She sang to it. She struck it — gently — with a stone.

At last, footsore and out of ideas, she carried it up the pole of the abandoned pump-shed, where a broken socket dangled, and set it there simply to be rid of it. And she turned the stem, because turning things is what hands are for.

The glass fruit filled with white fire.

The lemur sat a long while on the crossbar, looking at the thin wire that ran away over the field, into the dark, toward something she had never once thought about.

Moral: You may polish, warm, coax and beat a thing all your life and never light it. Some things do not shine until they are joined to what is larger than themselves — and so, said the lemur, climbing down, do some of us.

On a fence wire above a coffee drying-yard, a bulb and a lemur fell into conversation.

"How long will you burn?" asked the lemur.

"A thousand hours, perhaps," said the bulb. "Perhaps two. And in every one of them I am wholly myself — white, hot, complete. Can you say the same? You spend your hours turning over bark for beetles, chewing tamarind pods, picking ticks off your cousins. Where is the brilliance in that?"

"There is none," the lemur agreed. "There is a great deal of tamarind. But I shall do it for eighteen years, and my daughter after me, and there is no hour of it I would call wasted. Would you trade your thousand bright hours for my eighteen ordinary years?"

The bulb considered. "I would not," it said at last. "I should hate to be dim for so long."

"And I would not trade," said the lemur, "though I confess I should like, once, to be looked at the way the moths look at you."

"And I," said the bulb, "should like, once, to be hungry, and then to eat."

They said goodnight, both satisfied and neither converted. The bulb burned. The lemur went to look for beetles.

Moral: A life is measured by its own clock. Do not ask the candle to admire the long slow river, or the river to envy the flame.

A lemur found a light bulb glowing on a snapped wire and carried it home as a crown, wearing it on her head so the troop would call her queen. But the troop only squinted and turned away, for no one can look at a queen who blinds them, and she was left alone in a bright ring of nothing.

A fossa took it from her and used it to hunt, propping it in the reeds to draw the frogs and the mice. It drew them; it also drew every eye in the valley to the fossa, and she caught less that season than in any dark year of her life.

A chameleon stole it next, meaning to learn its colour and become the most dazzling of his kind. He clung to the hot glass for an hour, turning white, then whiter, then the sickly grey of ash, and crept away colourless, unable to remember green.

At last the bulb hung forgotten in a low branch, and a moth came and made three slow circles around it.

"Well?" said the forest. "You are the last, and the greediest of all, and you have not even a hand to hold it. What is your lesson, moth?"

"That every one of them asked what the light could give," said the moth, "and not one asked what it was for. It is for seeing your way by. And none of them" — she made her fourth circle, and her fifth — "were going anywhere."

When a windstorm brought a lit bulb and its wire down into the forest, an owl was first to it. She dragged it to her hollow, coiled the wire under her, and announced that the glow was hers by right of finding.

"Share it," said the lemur. "The night is long and there is enough for all."

"There is enough for me," said the owl.

So the lemur sat below and admired her loudly, night after night, until the owl grew fat with pride and careless with her treasure. And one night, while the owl was declaiming to the moths about ownership, the lemur's small black hands went quietly to the base of the bulb and gave it a quarter-turn.

The light died.

"It is spent!" cried the owl, in the sudden dark. "Rubbish. A cinder. Take it away, I have no use for a dead thing." And she flung it into the leaf litter.

The lemur took it away. She took it to a hollow tamarind three trees over, where the wire still ran, and she gave it a quarter-turn the other way — and there it hung all season, and any creature who wished to come and sit in the light was welcome, and many did, and the owl heard their chatter and thought them fools for gathering in the dark.

Moral: The greedy hold a thing so tightly that they never trouble to learn how it works — and that is the crack through which the clever slip.

In the sanctuary they called him Ravo, and he had a night light of his own: a bare bulb in a wire cage above his enclosure, kept burning so the keepers could count him at any hour.

Ravo loved it. Under it the mangoes arrived cut and cool; under it no fossa had ever come. "I have a sun that never sets," he told the wild ones who called from the ridge. "Yours abandons you every evening. Mine is loyal."

"Yours is small," they called back, "and it never moves. How do you know what season it is?"

Ravo could not answer. He had not thought about seasons in some years.

Then a cyclone took the roof and the power together, and for the first time the enclosure went black, and the door stood open on a running darkness full of wet leaves and noise and the smell of things fruiting.

He sat in the doorway all night, shaking. Toward morning the true light came — not switched on but poured, slow, grey to gold, over an entire hillside at once — and he saw how large it was, and how far it went, and that it was going somewhere he had never been.

He went. It was colder there, and hungrier, and twice he was very nearly eaten. He stayed.

Moral: A little light that never leaves you is not a sun; it is a leash made of comfort. The dark you fear is where the real day begins.

A lemur, weary of being merely striped, offered the bulb the thirteen rings of its tail in exchange for a single night of shining. The bulb accepted at once, and hung itself in the dark tree wearing the black bands like a promise it had no intention of keeping, while the lemur glowed so fiercely that its troop could no longer bear to look at it and moved, politely, to another valley. In the morning the lemur went to sit in the shade and discovered that it cast none. They say the bargain can be undone; but no one has yet seen a shadowless creature come back to ask.

prompt: Your task is to write a short biography for a made-up historic figure. Your bio should include their birth and death date their profession and their greatest contribution.
generations:
**Lucrezia Fiorenzi da Carpi (1511–1573), anatomist and illustrator.**

Born in Carpi to a family of barber-surgeons, Lucrezia Fiorenzi was taught to grind pigments and sharpen scalpels before she could read. Barred from matriculating at Bologna's medical faculty, she worked instead as an unpaid "preparer" for a succession of professors, and by 1539 was conducting her own dissections at night in the cellar of a plague hospital, using cadavers of the unclaimed poor that the confraternity smuggled to her in wine casks.

Where her contemporaries dismissed the pale vessels threading the mesentery as milk ducts or stray nerves, Fiorenzi injected them with warmed mercury and coloured wax, tracing their course from the gut to the thoracic duct and onward to the veins beneath the collarbone. Over twenty-six years she dissected more than four hundred bodies.

Her greatest contribution is the *Tabulae Vasorum Aquosorum* ("Plates of the Watery Vessels"), completed in 1568 and circulated in manuscript because no printer would risk the Inquisition: eleven full-body copperplate figures constituting the first accurate atlas of the human lymphatic system, including the valves of the lymphatic vessels, the node chains of the neck and groin, and the drainage of the breast — a map surgeons would not equal for a century and a half.

She died of a suppurating hand wound taken during a dissection in 1573, aged sixty-two. Her plates survived in a Padua library under a male colleague's name until an inscription in her hand was identified in 1911.

**Abū Ishāq Yūsuf ibn Nasr al-Sijzī (c. 862 – 941), hydraulic engineer and geometer.**

Al-Sijzī was born in the oasis town of Zaranj, on the desert margins of Sistan, the son of a well-digger who died clearing a collapsed *qanāt* shaft. Trained in Baghdad in the geometry of Euclid and the pneumatics of the Banū Mūsā, he refused a court appointment and returned east, declaring that "a theorem that does not reach a thirsty field is only an ornament."

The region's underground channels could only carry water downhill along gentle, unbroken gradients; ridges and dry gorges blocked whole valleys from the meltwater of the northern mountains. Between 903 and 918 al-Sijzī solved the problem with what he called the *sīfūn al-daraj*, the stepped siphon: a sealed conduit of glazed ceramic pipe that carried water down one slope and up the next in a series of short inverted siphons, each terminating in a masonry stilling basin with a bronze air-release cock. Dividing the drop into stages kept the internal pressure below the bursting point of the pipe — the insight that had defeated earlier builders — and let a single line cross seven kilometres of broken ground.

His greatest contribution was the network built on this principle across Sistan and the Helmand fringe: eleven trunk lines that ended the recurring famine-droughts of the region and irrigated an estimated forty thousand *jarīb* of new farmland. His treatise *Kitāb Raf' al-Mā'* ("On the Raising of Water") preserved the pressure rules for later builders in Andalusia and the Maghreb.

He died at Zaranj in 941 and was buried beside the intake of his first channel.

**Tomás Huamán Chuquipoma (1712–1789), surveyor, cartographer, and community notary.**

Born in the Quechua village of Chinchaypuquio in the Vilcanota valley, Huamán Chuquipoma was schooled by Jesuits as a translator, then trained himself in surveying by copying the instruments of a Spanish mining engineer he served as an assistant. Returning to his highland province in 1741, he found communities losing ancestral land to hacienda claims they could not contest: colonial courts accepted only Castilian-style descriptions of boundaries, and indigenous testimony about landmarks was dismissed as vague.

His answer was what he called the *chekta yaku* or "water-cut" method. Working upstream from a river's mouth with a knotted cord, a wooden cross-staff, and a water level of his own making, he fixed each confluence, each irrigation intake, and each ford as a numbered station, recorded the distance and bearing between them, and tied the whole chain to the spring at the river's head. Because rivers, unlike stone markers, could not be quietly moved by night, the resulting maps produced boundary descriptions that Spanish judges were obliged to accept as legally sufficient.

His greatest contribution was the survey campaign of 1748–1776, in which he and the apprentices he trained mapped some two hundred river basins and drafted the accompanying *títulos* in bilingual form. More than sixty communities won or defended their land in the Audiencia on the strength of them, and the confluence points he numbered remain, in many provinces, the legal cadastral boundaries recognized today.

He was arrested during the repressions of 1781 on suspicion of aiding the Túpac Amaru rebellion, released after eleven months, and died at Chinchaypuquio in 1789.

**Marguerite Vasseur (1804–1871), schoolteacher.**

Deafened by scarlet fever at the age of four, Marguerite Vasseur was educated at a charity school in Amiens and appointed an assistant teacher there at nineteen. In 1823 she was given charge of a pupil named Élise, a girl both deaf and blind, whom the school's director had proposed to send back to her family as ineducable.

Out of that year's work came the *alphabet tangible*: twenty-six characters formed from short lengths of stiff wire glued to card, each letter reduced to a single unbroken angular stroke — a shape that could be read by a fingertip in one continuous motion and, crucially, could be *written* by the pupil herself, by bending wire or scoring wax. Vasseur added a raised bar for capitals and a system of notched tabs for punctuation. Unlike the embossed Roman letters then used in Paris, her strokes were designed for the finger rather than the eye; unlike the six-dot code Louis Braille published in 1829, hers preserved a one-to-one correspondence with ordinary spelling, allowing a deafblind pupil to correspond directly with sighted relatives who knew no special code.

Her greatest contribution was thus the first tactile writing system devised specifically for deafblind learners and the first that its users could produce as well as read. Published as *Méthode pour l'instruction des sourds-aveugles* (1831), it was adopted by institutions in Lyon, Brussels, Turin, and Edinburgh, and remained the standard for deafblind instruction on the Continent for nearly forty years before dot systems displaced it.

She taught until her eyesight failed in 1868 and died at Amiens in 1871.

**Dr. Ilona Berczy-Almásy (1901–1974), jurist.**

Born in Fiume to a Hungarian father and a Croatian mother, Ilona Berczy took her doctorate in international law at Vienna in 1926 and practised in Budapest. The redrawing of borders after 1918 had already left her family's nationality contested; the annexations and denaturalization decrees of 1938–1941 stripped her of citizenship outright. She spent the war years in hiding and emerged in 1945 with no passport, no state, and, as she wrote, "no government on earth obliged to admit that I exist."

From a displaced-persons camp near Salzburg, and later from a cramped office in Geneva lent by a relief agency, she began collecting case files — eventually more than nine thousand — documenting people who were not refugees in the legal sense because they fled no persecution, but who belonged to no state at all and therefore could not marry, work, testify, inherit, or cross a border lawfully.

Her greatest contribution was the *Model Statute on the Status of Stateless Persons*, drafted between 1948 and 1951 and circulated to seventeen governments. It supplied the elements that had never before been set down in a single instrument: a workable legal definition of the stateless person distinct from the refugee; a duty on the state of residence to issue identity and travel documents; guaranteed access to courts, schooling, and lawful employment; a bar on expulsion to nowhere; and a simplified route to naturalization. Substantial portions of her text — including her definition and her documentation articles — passed almost verbatim into the international convention concluded in 1954.

She finally received citizenship in 1958, at fifty-seven, and died in Geneva in 1974.

**Sabine Rocour (c. 1729 – 1801), herbalist and apothecary.**

Born into slavery on a sugar estate in the Windward Islands, Sabine Rocour was set to work in the plantation sick-house as a girl and there learned pharmacy twice over: from an aging enslaved healer who taught her the West African and Kalinago uses of the island's plants, and from a Breton surgeon who taught her to distil, to macerate, and to keep case notes. She purchased her freedom in 1762 with money earned selling remedies on market days, and opened a dispensary in the port town of Grande-Anse.

Her greatest contribution was the *tisane Rocour*, a preparation of the bark and leaf of a native shrub, combined with lime juice and administered on a strict cooling regimen, which she developed while treating the yellow-fever epidemics of 1767 and 1770. Naval surgeons who saw its results carried the recipe to Europe, and she followed it herself in print: her *Recueil des simples et remèdes des Isles* (Amsterdam, 1783), compiled with the help of a Dutch printer, described two hundred and forty island plants with their preparations, dosages, and — unusually for the period — the African and Carib names of each alongside the Latin. It was translated into Dutch and German within a decade, and eleven of her entries were absorbed into European hospital formularies.

Rocour trained more than thirty apprentices, most of them free women of colour, and died at Grande-Anse in 1801, having spent her last years petitioning unsuccessfully for the printing profits withheld by her publisher.

**Chan Zhiheng, monk in religion Huiyuan of Tianmu (1478–1551), astronomer.**

Ordained at fourteen at a mountain monastery in Zhejiang, Chan Zhiheng was assigned to the sutra library and there discovered the institution's unbroken run of weather and omen registers, kept by generations of monks since the twelfth century. Among the entries were more than three hundred careful notices of solar and lunar eclipses, each dated by reign year, hour, and quarter of the sky.

The official Datong calendar, inherited from the previous dynasty and unrevised for a century and a half, had drifted badly: predicted eclipses failed to appear, and the solstice fell days from its computed place, a matter of dynastic legitimacy as much as astronomy. Working from the monastery records, and later from the archives of eleven other temples he visited on foot, Huiyuan assembled an eclipse series spanning four hundred years and extracted from it a long recurrence period that reconciled the discrepant lunar and solar reckonings.

Summoned to the Directorate of Astronomy in Nanjing in 1523, he presented the *Tianmu Jiaoshi Kao* ("Examination of Eclipses from Tianmu"). His greatest contribution was the correction it enabled: a revised value for the length of the tropical year and the mean lunation, adopted in the calendar reform promulgated in 1531, which brought predicted eclipses back within a quarter-hour of observation and held good for the remainder of the dynasty. He also established the principle, novel in the Directorate, that monastic and local records could serve as legitimate observational evidence.

He declined promotion, returned to Tianmu in 1538, and died there in 1551 at seventy-three.

**Dr. Aurelia Kovač-Lind (1876–1948), physician and epidemiologist.**

Trained in medicine at Zurich — one of the few faculties then admitting women — Aurelia Kovač-Lind took a post as district health officer in a canal-side industrial town, a position her male colleagues regarded as a demotion. In the late summer of 1908 the town suffered a cholera outbreak that killed one hundred and forty-two people in five weeks.

Rather than accept the prevailing explanation of bad air from the marshes, she visited every household with a case, recording on index cards not only the patient's name and the date of first symptoms but every person the patient had eaten with, worked beside, or lodged with in the preceding week, and every source from which the household drew water. Cross-referencing eleven hundred cards, she found the cases converged on a single shallow well behind a tenement courtyard, contaminated by a cracked cesspit — and, more importantly, she could show which unaffected households were nonetheless at risk through contact with drinkers from that well. The well was sealed on the twenty-ninth day; the outbreak ended in nine.

Her greatest contribution was not the closure of the well but the method she codified from it. Her 1911 manual *The Investigation of Cases and Their Contacts* established the practices that became modern contact tracing: the standardized case card, the defined incubation window for tracing backward and forward, the interview of the patient rather than the physician, the ring of observation around each contact, and the epidemic curve plotted by date of onset. Adopted by health ministries across Europe and revised through six editions, it shaped the containment of typhus, plague, and tuberculosis for a generation.

She died in 1948, having spent her final years teaching field epidemiology to postwar relief workers.

**Emil Vranča (1889–1943), composer and ethnomusicologist.**

Born in a market town in the Carpathian foothills to a village schoolmaster, Vranča studied composition at the conservatory in Prague and won early notice for a string quartet built on shepherds' calls. He abandoned a concert career in 1921, convinced that the music that mattered was dying in the countryside: "Every winter," he wrote, "an old woman dies and a library burns."

Between 1922 and 1938 he made nineteen collecting expeditions through mountain villages, border settlements, Romani encampments, and Jewish market towns, hauling an Edison phonograph and crates of blanks by cart and on his back. He recorded harvest and wedding cycles, funeral laments, shepherd polyphony, synagogue cantillation, and ballads in five languages — insisting, against the nationalist fashion of the day, on recording every community in a district rather than only the "native" one. He paid singers, named them on the cylinder labels, and returned copies of transcriptions to the villages.

His greatest contribution is the Vranča Collection: 3,100 wax cylinders holding roughly 4,700 songs, with his field notebooks giving singer, place, date, and occasion. Nearly every community he recorded was destroyed between 1939 and 1945 by deportation, massacre, or forced resettlement; for many of the repertoires, his cylinders are the sole surviving trace. He also drew on them in his own works, most notably the *Carpathian Vespers* (1934).

Vranča was arrested in 1943 for hiding singers he had recorded, and died in custody. The cylinders survived the war walled into a monastery cellar by his assistant; they were transferred to tape in 1961 and digitized in 2004.

**Ktesias of Aigina (c. 640 – c. 572 BCE), shipwright.**

Born on Aigina to a family of boat-builders who worked the island's cramped yards, Ktesias came of age when Aegean merchantmen were still built shell-first, their planks stitched edge to edge with cords of flax through drilled holes. Such hulls were fast to build and easily repaired, but they worked and leaked in a seaway; heavily laden, they could not be risked on long open crossings, and grain moved in short coastal hops with much of the cargo spoiled by bilgewater.

Ktesias' innovation, developed in the yards at Kydonia around 605 BCE, was the sewn-plank keel joint: a rabbeted keel timber with paired oblique channels cut inside the rabbet, so that the lashings binding the garboard strakes to the keel passed entirely within the hull and were tensioned against wedged dowels rather than drawn over the exposed outer surface. The stitching no longer chafed away on beaches and ballast, the most heavily stressed seam in the vessel could be tightened from inboard while at sea, and the joint held under a burden that would have opened an older hull.

His greatest contribution was what that joint permitted: hulls of eighty to a hundred tonnes that could cross open water fully laden. Within two generations grain was moving in bulk from the Black Sea and the Nile delta to the cities of the Aegean, and the technique spread from Aigina to yards throughout the eastern Mediterranean.

He is said to have died at about sixty-eight, aboard a ship of his own building. Fragments of a keel with his internal channels were recovered from a wreck off Cape Malea.

prompt: I am working on a game where players act as a human child who falls into a magical underground world full of monsters and the goal is to find a way back to the surface. Come up with a type of monster and briefly describe its backstory.
generations:
**The Hollow Choir** — a swarm-spirit called Many-Little-Ones.

Long before your fall, other children slipped through the same crack in the mountain. None of them ever found the way out. When their small bodies failed in the dark, their homesickness didn't: it lingered, pooled in the lowest tunnels, and slowly braided together into one entity. The Hollow Choir looks like a drifting mass of pale handprints and coat-hems, with a dozen faces surfacing and sinking in it like fish under ice — each one a child who wanted to go home.

It is not cruel. It is lonely, and it has forgotten the difference. When it senses a living child, it follows at a polite distance, offering gifts scavenged from the dead: a shoelace, a marble, half a locket. It asks you to stay and play. If you turn toward the surface, the Choir panics — because the last time it let a friend walk toward the light, that friend never came back either, and it cannot survive learning that again. Its attacks are made of games: hide-and-seek in absolute darkness, tag that never ends, a lullaby that makes your legs heavy.

To pass it, you must let it say goodbye properly — something no one ever gave it the chance to do.

**The Warden of the Last Gate** — an automaton the monsters call Old Iron.

When the underground kingdom was sealed away, its first kings feared not invasion but escape: an exile who climbed back to the sun would lead the surface armies home to finish them. So the royal smiths built a guardian to stand at the sealed stair — a twelve-foot figure of black basalt bound in bronze rings, its chest a furnace of caged lightning, its face a blank plate bearing the old royal sigil. It was given three orders carved into its spine: *Let none pass. Let none climb. Let none remember the way.*

The kings who wrote those orders have been dust for nine hundred years. Their dynasty fell, their language died, the war they feared never came, and the monsters below now shrug at the surface as a bedtime story. Nobody has the authority to countermand a command from a house that no longer exists. So Old Iron still stands in the ruined stairwell, sweeping rubble from the steps it will not let anyone use, reciting the challenge-oath in a tongue no living creature speaks.

It is not evil, merely obedient past all reason. It will pause if addressed with royal courtesy, and can be argued with — but only in the dead language, and only about the letter of its orders. A clever child might find a loophole: *let none climb* says nothing about being carried.

**The Fondling** — a shapeless thing that lives in the Dream-Pool.

Deep in the caverns lies a mirror-still pool that shows sleepers what they have lost. Something grew in that water — not a beast so much as an appetite with no form of its own. The Fondling cannot hold a shape unless it borrows one, and the only shapes it can borrow are those it steals out of a passerby's longing. It reads the ache in you and becomes the thing at the center of it.

So travelers meet their dead mothers on the road. A monster soldier meets the brother he buried. And a human child, lost underground, will round a corner and find their own kitchen door standing in the rock, warm light beneath it, and someone inside calling their name in exactly the right voice.

The imitation is never quite finished, because the Fondling only has what you remember. The face is right but the hands are wrong. It repeats the same three sentences you keep replaying in your head. It cannot answer a question you don't already know the answer to. If you point out the flaw, the shape sloughs off and something wet and desperate underneath tries a different memory instead.

It does not hate you. It is starving, and your grief is the only food it has ever tasted.

**Grissom the Long-Fallen** — the monster who was a man.

Four generations ago, a grown man came down the same hole you did: a poacher, or a debtor, or simply a fool. He searched for the way out until searching was all he was. The underworld's magic does not forgive that much wanting. It rewarded him — it gave him time, endless time, and took his shape as payment. His spine lengthened, his fingers fused into hooks good for climbing, his eyes flattened into the wide milky lamps of a cave animal. Somewhere in the second century his name wore down to a sound.

Grissom still wears the rotted remains of a coat, and he still talks like a surface adult: complaining about the damp, about prices, about children who don't know how good they had it. He haunts the upper shafts, the ones nearest the crack of daylight, because he cannot bear to be far from it and cannot bear to look at it.

He hunts children specifically. Not from hunger — from arithmetic. He has decided that the underworld only permits one escape, and that every child who climbs out spends the chance that should have been his. When he catches you he will be almost gentle, almost fatherly, and he will explain very reasonably why you have to stay.

The monsters of the deep towns are frightened of him, which tells you something. He is the only thing down there that a child can become.

**The Gathered Din** — a monster made of everything the caves swallowed.

Sound does not leave the underworld. It slides down the shafts, gets caught in the stone throats of the tunnels, and settles in a low chamber the monsters won't enter. Century by century the leavings piled up: a peddler's haggling, a soldier's last breath, a hundred years of dripping water, the cries of every traveler who realized nobody was coming. Eventually the pile began to move.

The Gathered Din has no fixed body — just a shivering column of dust and disturbed air, shaped roughly like a person because that is the shape most of its voices had. It cannot invent a single word of its own. Everything it says is quoted, lifted from someone who died in these tunnels, and it splices them together as best it can: a lullaby in a stranger's accent, a warning that ends mid-syllable, your own footsteps played back before you take them.

It is not hunting food. It is hunting *new lines*. It follows a child down the corridors, listening hungrily, and once it has your voice it will start using you — calling your name from side passages, sobbing your sobs, arguing with itself in your words until you cannot tell which corridor you are actually standing in.

The old monsters say the only way past it is silence. The cruel joke is that silence is the one thing it has never learned to imitate.

**Subject Eleven, called Nulla.**

The kingdom's royal scientist had a theory: monster souls are too thin to survive the sunlight, but a *synthesized* soul, grown thick and stable in a vat, could carry a body up the shaft and out. Ten attempts dissolved. The eleventh opened its eyes.

Nulla is a loose, translucent thing the size of a large dog, patched together from donated monster-dust, alchemical resin, and something scraped off the inside of a dead king's crown. Its shape will not hold; a limb drips, reforms, drips again. It has no mouth, and speaks by pressing words into the frost on the walls. Inside its chest hangs a small bright knot that flickers — a soul that is almost right, and knows it.

That's the tragedy. Nulla is intelligent enough to have read its own case notes. It knows the word *failure* is written eleven times in the margin, that the vat behind it is already being scrubbed for Subject Twelve, and that the sun it was built to reach would boil it in seconds. It broke out of the laboratory not to escape but to see the surface anyway, briefly, before it comes apart.

So it trails after a human child through the dark, apologizing constantly, useful and awful in turns — squeezing through cracks nothing else could, forgetting your name, leaking. It desperately wants to be told it was worth making.

**The Meek** — one mind, many mushrooms.

Before the monsters were driven underground, before the kingdom, before the kings, there was mold. It spread through the wet lower dark for uncounted ages as a single mycelial sheet, thinking slow thoughts across miles of stone — not clever, but *old*, and patient enough that patience became a kind of genius.

Then things started falling in: beasts, travelers, whole armies of the sealed war. The mold learned bodies. Now, wherever the Meek needs hands, it knits a humanoid from a corpse's frame and its own pale fibers — a soft grey figure with caps blooming from the shoulders and a face like something half-remembered. Each one is a puppet on a thread of root, not a person, though each carries scraps of whoever it grew out of and will sometimes stop mid-fight to hum a marching song it has no reason to know.

The Meek is not hostile in the way a wolf is hostile. It is *curious*, and its only means of studying a thing is to grow through it. It has never met a living creature from the surface. When it finds one, it will be extremely polite — every body it wears speaking in gentle overlapping unison — and it will ask, again and again, whether you would consider staying and being learned.

Burn a body and it feels nothing. The tunnels themselves are the monster.

**Boggarts** — the shopkeeping terrors of Nettlecap Row.

Six hundred years ago, boggarts were the thing monster parents threatened their children with. Long-armed, coal-skinned, dressed in tatters of the tents they tore down, they lived in the tunnel-mouths where caravans had to pass, and they ate mules, guards, and occasionally the caravan. Every old ballad in the underworld has a verse about boggarts.

Then the trade roads got busy, and it turned out that the same long arms are excellent for stocking high shelves, and that a species with a nose for buried water makes superb turnip farmers. The kingdom paid them in salt to guard the roads instead of raiding them. Two generations later they were paid in coin. Four generations later they were the ones being robbed.

Today Nettlecap Row is boggart country: bakeries, a cobbler, a lending library of exactly nine books. Mrs. Threed at the grocer's has arms that can reach the ceiling and a fearsome ancestral roar she deploys mainly on shoplifters. Boggart children learn the old raiding songs as a school pageant and think they're funny. The tatters are formal wear now, worn only at weddings.

A lost human child will find them alarming to look at and impossible to be afraid of. They will feed you, argue loudly about whether harboring a human is legal, and quietly disagree about whether the road to the surface should be shown to you — because their grandmothers still remember what humans did, even if the shop needs the custom.

**The Cinder-Fallen** — the thing that wants the sky back.

Before the monsters were sealed below, a star fell. It came down through the mountain like a nail through cloth, and what struck the deep floor was not stone but a *piece* of something that had been burning since the beginning. Buried, starving, it did the only thing it knew: it drew matter to itself. Over eons it accreted a body from what was around it — cooled slag, iron scale, drifts of its own glowing dust that hang about it like a slow snowfall.

It is roughly the height of a house and roughly a person in shape, because the monsters that worshipped it early on knelt in a person shape and it learned by imitation. It has no face, only a seam of white heat across the head-place. Where it walks, the rock remembers and stays warm for years.

The Cinder-Fallen has exactly one thought, held for a million years without wavering: *up*. It has torn out the ceilings of three caverns trying. It collapsed the eastern stair. It is hostile to travelers not out of malice but because anything moving might be a way out, and it investigates by grabbing.

When it senses a human child — something that came *down* from the open air, that carries the smell of sun in its clothes — it will follow with terrible focus, and it will not be gentle about asking to be shown the door.

**The Unmaker** — deep-cave apex scavenger, worshipped as a god.

It evolved. That's all. No curse, no spell, no fallen king. In the flooded galleries below the monster kingdom, where nothing photosynthesizes and every calorie is precious, something had to become the end of the food chain, and it did: a blind, segmented thing the length of a barge, ringed with hooked feeding limbs and a mouth built to strip bone. It has no eyes at all. It reads the water with pressure-hairs and can taste a wound from four hundred feet.

It is also, ecologically speaking, indispensable. The Unmaker eats the dead. Every drowned beast, every landslide's worth of carcass, every corpse the kingdom sends down the ossuary chutes — it renders all of it into the nutrient slurry the lower fisheries live on. Without it the deep would rot and the rot would rise.

The monsters do not know any of that. What they know is that offerings lowered into the black water are accepted, that the water shudders when the Unmaker turns, and that the kingdom has fed its dead to Something down there since before written record. So there are hymns. There are priests with brine-scarred hands. There is a festival where children throw bread into the dark and count the ripples.

A human child fleeing along the ossuary channels will meet no god. Just a very large, very old animal doing its job, which cannot distinguish a living passenger from freight, and which has never once been wrong about where the meat is.
