Buy it unlocked, skip the insurance plan you'd otherwise need, and expect the same phone to still be working in four years. If HMD's rugged line has since updated, buy the current XR model.

**Best first phone: the Light Phone III.**

Every other choice on the market asks a teenager to win a fight that adults routinely lose — sitting with an infinite scroll in their pocket and voluntarily putting it down. The Light Phone III removes the fight instead of managing it.

It's a real, unlocked 5G phone with a small black-and-white matte screen. It does calls, texts, an alarm, a calculator, notes, turn-by-turn directions, a music/podcast player, a basic camera and a Wi-Fi hotspot. There is no web browser, no app store, no social media, no video feed, no notification firehose. You are not installing a monitoring app or negotiating screen-time limits, because there is nothing to monitor: the hardware simply cannot deliver TikTok at 1 a.m.

That matters most precisely at the age when a first phone is handed over. The reason parents want their kid reachable — late practice, missed bus, ride home — is fully satisfied by calls, texts and maps. Everything else in a smartphone is what they'll later ask you to help them cut back on. Giving a phone whose entire purpose is communication also sets an honest expectation: this is a tool, not entertainment, and a full smartphone is something you graduate into at 16 or 17 after demonstrating you can manage a schedule and a group chat without it eating you.

Practical notes before you buy: it works with your own SIM or eSIM on major U.S. carriers, so it slots into an existing family plan. It costs more than a $150 Android — you're paying for restraint, not silicon — so weigh that honestly. And be candid with your teen: no Instagram, no YouTube, no group video chats, and school apps that require a smartphone won't run, so check what your school requires first.

If you want one device that keeps a kid reachable without handing them the entire internet on day one, this is it.

**Best first phone: the Samsung Galaxy A16 5G.**

Pick a first phone on the metric that actually decides when it becomes garbage: software support. Cheap phones don't usually die because the chip got slow — they die because the manufacturer stops shipping security patches, banking and school apps drop support, and the thing quietly becomes unsafe to carry. Samsung broke that pattern at the bottom of the market: the Galaxy A16 5G, launched around $200 in the U.S., is promised six generations of Android OS upgrades and six years of security updates. Hand it to a 13-year-old and it's still a patched, supported phone when they leave for college.

That combination — two hundred dollars plus six years — is the whole argument. A first phone will be dropped, sat on, left on a bleacher and possibly swum with, so you want the loss to be an annoyance rather than an insurance claim. At this price you can replace it outright and still have spent less than one flagship. But you also don't want to be re-buying every 18 months, and cheap phones from most other brands force exactly that.

The rest is unglamorous and adequate: a large Super AMOLED screen that's genuinely nice for the money, a 5,000 mAh battery that survives a school day plus practice, a headphone jack, expandable storage via microSD, a fingerprint sensor, and 5G so it isn't stranded as carriers retire older networks. It has light water resistance, not a rugged rating — add a case and a screen protector on day one.

On the parenting side, being an Android means Google Family Link works natively: app approval, screen-time limits, location sharing, and content filters you control from your own phone, free.

Be clear-eyed about the trade-offs: photos are ordinary in low light, charging is slow-ish, and heavy 3D games will stutter. None of that determines whether a first phone was a good purchase. Longevity per dollar does, and this wins it.

prompt: What's a cool fact about the city of Pittsburgh?
generations: Pittsburgh is nicknamed the "City of Bridges" for good reason: there are 446 bridges within the city limits, more than any other city on Earth. That's more than Venice, Italy, and more than Hamburg, Germany, the two cities usually cited as rivals for the title. The count includes everything from the soaring steel of the Fort Pitt Bridge to tiny spans over ravines and rail lines, a consequence of a city carved up by three rivers, dozens of creeks, and steep hillsides that force roads to leap rather than climb.

Pittsburgh sits at one of North America's great watery crossroads: at Point State Park, the Allegheny River flowing down from New York and the Monongahela River flowing up from West Virginia collide to form the Ohio River. That makes the city a continental drainage gateway, since a raindrop landing downtown can travel the Ohio into the Mississippi and out to the Gulf of Mexico, some 1,900 miles away. That geography is precisely why the French and British fought over the spot in the 1750s and why the city grew where it did.

At the height of the steel era, the Pittsburgh region poured out roughly half of all steel made in the United States, arming two world wars and framing skyscrapers nationwide. The price was air so thick with soot that streetlights burned at midday and office workers changed shirts by lunchtime. Visiting in 1868, journalist James Parton famously described looking down from Mount Washington at the flaring mills and called Pittsburgh "hell with the lid taken off" — a phrase the city has never quite lived down.

Here's the twist on Pittsburgh's smoky reputation: the former "Smoky City" has repeatedly been ranked among America's most livable cities by outfits like The Economist's Global Liveability rankings and Places Rated Almanac. It also became a green-building leader, with one of the highest concentrations of LEED-certified square footage per capita in the country. The David L. Lawrence Convention Center was the world's first LEED-certified convention center, and PNC's downtown tower was billed as the greenest office skyscraper in the world when it opened in 2015.

Pittsburgh is where polio was beaten. Working in a lab at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine from 1947 onward, Jonas Salk and his team developed the first successful polio vaccine, using killed virus. After a massive field trial involving nearly two million American schoolchildren, the vaccine was declared safe and effective on April 12, 1955 — news that set church bells ringing across the country. Salk famously declined to patent it, reportedly asking, "Could you patent the sun?"

Pittsburgh has an outsized claim on how we communicate. On November 2, 1920, station KDKA broadcast returns from the Harding–Cox presidential election from a shack atop the Westinghouse plant in East Pittsburgh, an event widely credited as the world's first commercial radio broadcast. Six decades later, on September 19, 1982, Carnegie Mellon computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed using :-) and :-( on a campus message board to mark jokes and non-jokes — the birth of the emoticon, ancestor of every emoji on your phone.

Pittsburgh punches far above its weight in screen culture. Fred Rogers made "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood" at WQED, the nation's first community-sponsored public television station, and its trolley and Neighborhood of Make-Believe were built in studios there. In 1967–68, a young George A. Romero and his local ad-film crew shot "Night of the Living Dead" on a shoestring in and around the city, using a farmhouse near Evans City and a Pittsburgh-area cemetery — essentially inventing the modern zombie genre out of western Pennsylvania.

Pittsburgh is the only city in the United States whose major professional sports teams all wear the same colors: the Steelers (NFL), Penguins (NHL), and Pirates (MLB) all suit up in black and gold. It isn't a coincidence or a copycat move — the palette comes from the city's official flag and coat of arms, which borrow the black and gold of William Pitt's family crest. The Pirates switched to match in 1948, and the Penguins adopted it in 1980, cementing the citywide look.

Pittsburgh still runs 19th-century funicular railways as everyday transit. The Monongahela Incline (1870) and the Duquesne Incline (1877) haul passengers up the near-vertical face of Mount Washington in wooden cable cars — remnants of a system that once included around 20 inclines built to carry mill workers home up hillsides too steep for horses. The city also maintains more than 700 sets of public outdoor staircases, thousands of steps in all, and some of them are legally designated as city streets, complete with street signs and addresses.

Pittsburgh's food scene has a genuine architectural quirk: at Primanti Bros., a sandwich arrives with the french fries and vinegary coleslaw stacked *inside* the Italian bread alongside the meat and cheese — a Strip District innovation from the 1930s meant to feed truckers a one-handed meal. Western Pennsylvania has other credits, too: the Big Mac was invented in 1967 by franchisee Jim Delligatti in Uniontown, southeast of the city, and the banana split was created in 1904 by apprentice pharmacist David Strickler in Latrobe.

prompt: What's an uncool fact about the city of Pittsburgh?
generations: At the height of its steel era, Pittsburgh was so choked with coal and coke smoke that downtown streetlights had to burn at noon and office workers changed soot-blackened shirts midday. Visiting writer James Parton famously described the view of the city's furnaces as "hell with the lid off," a nickname that stuck for generations. It's an uncool reminder that the region's industrial wealth was literally paid for in breathable air.

The pollution didn't leave with the mills. Southwestern Pennsylvania still carries an unusually heavy burden of asthma, respiratory disease and lung cancer risk tied to decades of coke-oven and mill emissions, and Allegheny County continues to earn failing or near-failing grades in the American Lung Association's annual "State of the Air" rankings for particle pollution—driven in part by the Clairton Coke Works, the largest such plant in North America. For a city marketed as a green tech hub, that's a decidedly uncool asterisk.

Pittsburgh's economy didn't gently transition—it cratered. Beginning in the late 1970s, the collapse of Big Steel wiped out well over 100,000 regional manufacturing jobs in barely a decade, and mill towns strung along the Monongahela like Homestead, Duquesne, Braddock and Aliquippa lost their economic reason for existing. Unemployment in parts of the Mon Valley hit Depression-era levels, and many of those communities have never recovered their tax base or main streets.

Pittsburgh is a city that shrank by more than half. It counted roughly 676,000 residents in the 1950 census; today the city proper is home to only about 300,000. That long hollowing-out left behind thousands of vacant lots, abandoned houses and closed school buildings, and it means much of the city's infrastructure—water lines, sewers, streets—was built for twice the population now paying to maintain it.

For years Pittsburgh was one of the oldest metropolitan areas in the United States by median age, rivaled mainly by Florida retirement regions—and it recorded more deaths than births for a long stretch, meaning the population declined through natural causes alone. That grim statistic was the demographic fingerprint of a generation of young people who left after high school or college because the jobs went away, leaving their parents and grandparents behind.

Pittsburgh's own 2019 Gender Equity Commission report delivered a brutal verdict: Black residents, and Black women in particular, fare worse in Pittsburgh than in most comparable American cities on measures like maternal and infant mortality, poverty, employment and health outcomes. The researchers noted that a Black woman would likely have better life outcomes in nearly any other similar city. The "most livable city" accolades, in other words, have not applied equally to everyone who lives here.

The 1892 Homestead Strike, just up the Monongahela from downtown, ended in a pitched gun battle on July 6 between locked-out steelworkers and barge-loads of armed Pinkerton detectives hired by Carnegie Steel, leaving roughly ten men dead and dozens wounded. The state militia occupied the town, the union was broken, and organized labor was effectively shut out of the American steel industry for the next four decades—a bloody, uncool chapter beneath the Carnegie name on the city's libraries and concert hall.

The Pittsburgh region has an ugly record of catastrophe. In 1889 the failure of a private club's dam sent a wall of water into Johnstown, killing about 2,200 people in one of the deadliest disasters in U.S. history. In 1948 a temperature inversion trapped mill fumes over Donora, roughly 25 miles down the Monongahela, killing 20 people in a few days and sickening thousands. And in March 1936 the St. Patrick's Day flood put downtown Pittsburgh under as much as 20 feet of water.

Pittsburgh's beloved bridge count—446 spans, more than any other city in the world—comes with a dark flip side: a large share of them, along with hundreds more across the county, have been rated in poor or structurally deficient condition, with maintenance repeatedly deferred for lack of money. The consequences turned literal on January 28, 2022, when the Fern Hollow Bridge in Frick Park simply collapsed into the ravine below, dropping a city bus and several cars and injuring ten people.

Pittsburgh is one of the cloudiest major cities in the United States. It averages roughly 200 overcast or mostly cloudy days a year and only around 160 with meaningful sunshine, receiving less than half the possible sunlight annually—worse than famously gray Seattle by some measures. From November through March the sky is a near-permanent flat gray, which is why seasonal affective disorder and vitamin D deficiency are running local jokes that aren't entirely jokes.

prompt: What's the one best thing about going on a vacation?
generations: The single best thing about a vacation is that nothing is owed. No inbox, no deadline, no meeting you must be alert for, no chore whose deferral will cost you later. Ordinary life is a mesh of small obligations, each one minor, all of them constantly pulling at your attention; a vacation is the rare interval when that pull simply stops. The value isn't in what you do instead — you may do very little, and it still works. It's the absence of demand itself that feels like relief, the way silence feels loud after a long noise. For a week, no one needs anything from you at a particular hour. That negative freedom, being unclaimed, is the good that no weekend or evening can supply, and it is the thing worth paying for.

The best thing about a vacation is that you get the people you love with their whole attention, and they get yours. At home, the same family occupies the same rooms and still passes each other in fragments: someone's on a call, someone's driving to practice, someone's half-listening while cooking. Away, the ordinary machinery that splits you up isn't there. You end up in a car, on a beach towel, at one long dinner table with nothing scheduled after it, and conversations start that would never have room to start at home — the long story, the confession, the running joke that becomes family vocabulary for years. What you bring back isn't a tan; it's a stock of shared references and a relationship that has been given actual, uninterrupted hours. That closeness is the real souvenir.

The best thing about going away is discovering how many other ways there are to be a human being. A market that opens at dawn and smells of herbs you can't name; a language whose sounds your mouth has to learn; strangers who greet, eat, argue and rest on a schedule nobody at home would recognize. Every one of these is quietly informative: it shows you that some habit you assumed was simply correct is only local. Travel widens the sample size of your life. You come back with a bigger internal map — more foods you can imagine, more ways a street can be laid out, more solutions to the problem of living. That expansion of what seems possible is permanent, and no photograph or documentary delivers it the way standing in an unfamiliar place does.

The best thing about a vacation is that your body finally gets to catch up. Most of us run a small chronic deficit — an hour of sleep short each night, muscles braced, a nervous system that never fully leaves standby. Given a few days with no alarm and no reason to be anywhere, that quietly reverses. You sleep ten hours the first night and are shocked at it. By day four you wake before the alarm you didn't set, your shoulders have dropped an inch, headaches you'd stopped noticing are gone, and your appetite and digestion behave normally again. This is real physiological repair, not a mood. It's why you can return to the same job and same commute and cope with them completely differently. Being genuinely restored, rather than merely distracted, is the benefit that lasts longest.

The best thing about leaving home is what the distance shows you about home. Inside your routine, you can't see the routine — you're too busy executing it. A few hundred miles away, with none of the usual cues, the shape of your life becomes visible: which parts you missed within two days, which parts you didn't think about once, which relationship you kept wanting to tell things to, which obligation you dreaded resuming. That information is almost impossible to get while you're immersed. People quit jobs, move cities, propose, or finally end things on the strength of a clarity that arrived on a train or a balcony. Vacation is the only regular opportunity most adults have to stand outside their own life and evaluate it. The view is the point.

The best thing about a vacation is being returned to your senses. For a stretch of days, your body is allowed to enjoy itself for no reason at all: the shock of cold water and then the warmth of stone afterwards, salt drying on your arms, a long lunch eaten slowly because there is nothing to be late for, fruit at the right ripeness, the specific pleasure of sleeping with a window open to unfamiliar night air. Ordinary life routes almost all physical experience through purpose — food eaten fast, exercise done for metrics, sun caught between errands. On vacation, pleasure stops justifying itself. Swimming isn't training, dinner isn't fuel, and the afternoon isn't an input to anything. That unhurried, purposeless bodily enjoyment is the most immediate happiness available to an adult, and vacation is where it's permitted.

The best thing about a vacation is the empty hours. A long stretch of unstructured time — an afternoon with no plan, a rainy day, a four-hour train, a wait for a ferry — is where the mind starts doing things it never does when it's busy. You get mildly bored, and then curious: you notice the building across the street, wander down a street for no reason, pick up a book you'd never have chosen, and somewhere in there an idea arrives about a problem you weren't consciously working on. Solutions and half-formed projects surface in exactly these gaps. Everyday life is engineered to eliminate them; every dull minute gets filled. Vacation restores the vacancy, and vacancy is the raw material of creativity and spontaneity. The trip's best moments are usually the unplanned ones that only unplanned time can produce.

The best thing about a vacation happens before you leave. From the moment it's booked, you own a piece of the future: a folder of half-mad plans, a map you keep opening, arguments about which town to stay in, a phrase you've decided to learn. Happiness research on this is fairly blunt — the measurable lift shows up strongly in the anticipation phase, and it can run for weeks, brightening Tuesdays that would otherwise be indistinguishable. Anticipation is also uncontaminated: the imagined trip has no delayed flights, no rain, no sunburn, no argument at the rental desk. And unlike the trip, it lasts. Ten days of travel bought you two months of looking forward. That prospective glow, the sense that something good is coming, is the most reliable and best-value thing a vacation delivers.

The best thing about a vacation is that nobody there knows who you are. At home you're a fixed character — reliable one, quiet one, the person who doesn't dance and doesn't order dessert — and everyone's expectations keep quietly enforcing it. Among strangers, none of that is loaded. You can wear the loud shirt, talk to people at the next table, sing badly at karaoke, sign up for the diving course, tell your story with a different emphasis, sit alone in a café all morning without anyone asking if you're all right. Nothing gets reported back. Some of what you try is silly and stays abroad; occasionally you discover you actually like being that version of yourself and bring it home. Either way, the temporary suspension of your own reputation is a freedom you can get almost nowhere else.

The best thing about a vacation is coming back. Two weeks away performs a trick nothing else can: it makes the utterly familiar strange again, and therefore visible. Your own bed feels engineered specifically for your spine. Your kitchen, where every knife and spice is exactly where your hand expects it, is suddenly a marvel of convenience. The tap water tastes right. Your dog's greeting is disproportionate and perfect. Walking your own street, you notice the tree on the corner and the good bakery you'd stopped registering years ago. Absence resets the adaptation that had quietly stripped the pleasure out of all of it. Going away is, in this sense, an investment in liking your ordinary life more — and since ordinary life is where you'll spend the other fifty weeks, that renewed appreciation is far and away the most valuable thing the trip provides.

prompt: What is the absolute worst thing about being a graduate student?
generations: The worst thing is that your entire professional life hangs on the goodwill of one person. Your advisor controls the grant that pays you, the lab space and data you need, whose name goes first on the paper, whether your chapters are "ready," when you're allowed to defend, and — for years afterward — the letter that determines whether anyone hires you. No other adult relationship concentrates that much leverage in a single individual with so little oversight. There is no HR department that will meaningfully cross a tenured faculty member who brings in funding. There is no transfer market: switching advisors usually means losing years of work, and switching programs often means starting over entirely, if you're admitted at all. Even a well-meaning advisor's neglect — unanswered emails, a draft sat on for five months — can cost you a job cycle, and you cannot complain, because the person you'd complain about is also the person who writes the letter. So you learn to manage upward constantly: reading moods, softening disagreements, absorbing credit losses in silence, agreeing to projects you know are dead ends. That daily self-censorship is corrosive in a way that's hard to explain to people outside. You entered academia to argue freely about ideas, and instead you spend six years being extremely careful about what you say to one specific person, because they hold every exit.

The worst thing is being paid too little to live on during exactly the years when everyone else is compounding. A stipend of roughly $25,000–$35,000 in a city where rent alone eats half of it means you are working sixty-hour weeks and still doing arithmetic at the grocery store at thirty-one years old. Summers are frequently unfunded, so you scramble for a teaching section or an adjunct gig, or you simply eat three months of savings you don't have. Meanwhile the arrangement is explicitly not merit-based: you can publish three papers, win a teaching award, and bring in an external grant, and your pay stays exactly the same as the person down the hall who did nothing, because your "salary" is a line item, not a wage. There is no raise, no bonus, no negotiation. And the damage is invisible and cumulative: no employer 401(k) match, no home equity, no Social Security credits worth anything, sometimes new loans for the fees your stipend doesn't cover. Six years of not saving in your late twenties isn't six years of lost income; it's decades of lost compounding. You emerge with a doctorate, a negative net worth, and a peer group that bought houses. The insult is that everyone around you frames it as an honor rather than as underpayment, so asking for more feels like admitting you were never really in it for the ideas.

The worst thing is that there is no end date, and nobody will give you one. A job has a start; a degree program has a nominal length that everyone quietly knows is fiction. You are told "about five years" and you watch people finish in eight. Every milestone that looks like a finish line turns out to be a movable object: the qualifying exam gets rescheduled, the committee member on sabbatical can't read your prospectus until spring, the reviewer wants another experiment, your advisor decides the third chapter "isn't there yet" — and "there" is never defined in writing. You cannot plan anything. You cannot sign a two-year lease with confidence, accept a wedding invitation abroad, tell a partner when you can move, or apply for jobs, because the honest answer to "when do you graduate?" is "I don't know, ask someone else." Your timeline is not yours; it is a function of another person's inbox, travel schedule, and standards, none of which you can audit or appeal. The psychological effect is worse than the logistical one. Effort stops feeling connected to progress, because you can work brilliantly for six months and be exactly as close to finishing as before. That's the corrosive part: living for years inside an open-ended sentence, always about eighteen months from done, and having been about eighteen months from done for four years.

The worst thing is what it does to your head. Graduate programs report depression and anxiety at rates several times the general population's, and the structure of the work almost seems engineered to produce it. You are selected for being the best student anyone had ever seen, then placed in a room where everyone was, so your entire self-concept is suddenly evidence-free. Feedback is overwhelmingly negative by design — peer review, committee comments, seminar critique — so the daily signal is failure, while success arrives in rare, delayed, ambiguous lumps. Impostor syndrome isn't an occasional wobble; it's the ambient condition, the constant sense that admission was a clerical error about to be discovered. What makes it the *worst* thing rather than merely a hard thing is the stigma layered on top. Struggling is coded as not being cut out for it. You hesitate to use the counseling center because the waitlist is ten weeks and because you half-believe someone will hear. You don't tell your advisor you're not sleeping, because the person you'd tell also decides your future. So the illness gets managed privately, badly, at 2 a.m., while you perform competence in seminar. People leave with a doctorate and a genuine, lasting psychiatric injury, and the culture's response is to admire how hard the survivors worked.

The worst thing is that there is no version of you that isn't the work, so there is never a moment that is genuinely off. A dissertation isn't a set of tasks you complete and put down; it's a question you carry, and it runs in the background during dinner, in the shower, on holiday, at your friend's wedding. Nobody clocks you out. There is no Friday, because Saturday has exactly the same obligations, and no one will stop you from working through both. Worse, the boundary doesn't just blur — it disappears in the wrong direction. Because the work is an expression of your mind, criticism of the argument feels like criticism of your character, and a stalled chapter feels like a personal moral failure rather than a technical problem. Rest becomes impossible to actually enjoy: an afternoon off is not restorative, it's a debt, and you spend it composing a defense of why you deserved it. People describe finishing a novel or a big project and going home; there is no home to go to here, because the project has annexed the house. And when someone asks who you are, you say the name of your subfield. Five years in, you realize you have no hobbies, no identity that survives a bad result, and no idea what you'd be if the thesis failed — which means you can never afford to let it.

The worst thing is being structurally nothing — neither an employee nor really a student, and therefore covered by neither set of protections. You teach two sections, grade two hundred exams, run a lab, and write grant text that gets submitted under someone else's name: that's labor. But you are classified as a trainee, so labor law, overtime rules, workplace-harassment procedures, and unemployment insurance often don't apply cleanly to you, and in many places the right to bargain collectively has been litigated for decades precisely because nobody can say what you are. Meanwhile you're not a real student either: you pay fees for services you never use, you're excluded from undergraduate support structures, and "academic" grievance processes are designed for disputes about grades, not about being worked eighty hours a week. The practical consequences are concrete. Parental leave is a favor rather than a policy. Health insurance is a plan you're auto-enrolled in and can't change. If you're injured, if you're harassed by a PI, if your funding vanishes mid-year, the institution's first act is to check which category you fall into — and the answer is a shrug. You get the obligations of a job and the powerlessness of a pupil, plus the deference expectations of both. Falling through a gap you didn't know existed, and being told there's no office for that, is worse than any single indignity.

The worst thing is the possibility, present every single day, that none of it will amount to anything — and that the years are non-refundable. You bet five or six years of your life on one question, chosen when you knew the least, and the bet can lose in several ways. The technique may simply not work, and you find out in year four. A better-resourced lab publishes your result while your paper is in revision, and overnight your central contribution becomes a citation in someone else's introduction. Or, most quietly devastating, the project succeeds exactly as planned and turns out to be trivial — a small, true, uninteresting thing that nobody needed. There is no partial credit in the outside world for "I spent four years learning that this doesn't work." You cannot recover the time, and there is no insurance, no severance, no version of the sunk cost that converts to something else. What makes this the worst part is that you have to keep working anyway, with full commitment, while holding the live possibility of futility in your mind. Every difficult stretch carries the second-order fear: not just "is this hard?" but "is this real, or have I built a career on a mirage?" Ordinary jobs can be boring or badly paid; few of them let you discover at thirty-two that your entire twenties produced nothing anyone will ever read.

The worst thing is watching your life get postponed while everyone else's starts. At twenty-two you're all in roughly the same place. At thirty, your friends have equity in a house, a job title with a ladder attached, and the ability to answer "where will you live in two years?" You have a stipend, an apartment you can't decorate because you might move, and the standing possibility that your next step is a one-year position in a state you've never visited. Everything that constitutes adult life gets pushed behind the degree. You don't buy property because you can't get a mortgage on fellowship income and won't stay. You have the children conversation and end it with "after I finish," year after year, while the biology doesn't wait. Your partner's career gets subordinated to a job market that will send you both somewhere neither of you chose, or you agree to be apart for a while, and "a while" becomes four years. You skip the reunion because the flight is a week of groceries. The cruelty isn't the deprivation itself, which is survivable; it's the asymmetry made visible on your phone every day. You are not behind because you failed. You are behind because you did exactly what was asked, brilliantly, for a decade — and the reward structure delayed every ordinary marker of a settled life until an age when your friends are already renovating theirs.

The worst thing is that the people who should be your closest allies are also your competitors, and everyone knows the arithmetic. Your cohort enters together, takes the same seminars, and is trained explicitly for a professoriate that will absorb maybe a quarter of you, in fields where a single tenure-track posting draws three hundred applications. So every shared space becomes a scoreboard. Who got the external fellowship. Who has a first-author paper by year three. Who got invited to the conference panel, whose advisor is actually connected, who got the interview at the school you also applied to. You congratulate people sincerely and feel something ugly underneath, then feel worse about feeling it. It poisons the ordinary business of intellectual life: you get vague about your methods in the hallway, you don't share the dataset, you sit on the good idea until it's safely submitted. Collaboration becomes strategic rather than joyful, and the seminar — supposedly the place where you think out loud — becomes a performance where admitting confusion is a tactical error. And it is genuinely zero-sum at the end. When two of you make the same shortlist, one gets a career and the other gets adjuncting. Spending your late twenties being quietly measured against the only people who understand your work, and knowing that most of you will lose, is lonelier than any amount of overwork.

The worst thing is the deliberate narrowing — the way a mind that could have gone anywhere gets spent, at its sharpest, on one very small thing. You arrive in love with a whole field. Within two years you are told, correctly, that you cannot be interesting in general and must become the world expert in something specific, and specific means small: a subclause in a legal doctrine, a protein's behavior in one mutant line, a decade in one provincial archive. Then for years that is nearly all you read, nearly all you think, and nearly all you're allowed to say anything about. The cost isn't just boredom. It's what you didn't learn. You spend your most plastic, energetic intellectual years acquiring a skill set with an extremely narrow market, while the languages you wanted to learn, the second discipline you wanted to read into, the code you never wrote, all go unclaimed — and you can feel your curiosity contracting to fit the aperture. The final indignity is the readership. Median citations for a dissertation hover near zero; realistically your five committee members, three reviewers, and a handful of specialists will ever engage with the thing you gave a decade to. Trading breadth for depth would be a fine bargain if the depth were shared. Discovering that you narrowed almost to a point, mostly for an audience of six, is the part that stings.

prompt: Name the place you think is the top vacation destination in the world.
generations: Paris, France. No other city concentrates so much of what people actually travel for inside so small a walkable footprint. In an afternoon you can stand before the Winged Victory and the Mona Lisa at the Louvre, walk to Sainte-Chapelle's stained glass, cross the Seine on foot, and still make a 7:30 dinner. The architecture is a continuous, legible record from Roman baths at Cluny to Haussmann's boulevards to the Pompidou, and it is preserved as a living city rather than a museum quarter. The food culture operates at every price point: a three-euro baguette from an award-winning boulangerie is as characteristically Parisian as a Michelin-starred tasting menu, and the neighborhood market on rue Mouffetard or the Marché d'Aligre gives visitors real access to it. The Métro makes a car pointless. Parks — Luxembourg, Buttes-Chaumont, the Tuileries — mean you can spend a day doing nothing expensive and still feel you spent it well. And Paris rewards return visits differently than a beach does: the museums rotate, the seasons change the light on the limestone, and the city has an unrivalled talent for making ordinary hours — coffee at a zinc bar, a walk along the Canal Saint-Martin at dusk — feel like the point of the trip rather than the gaps between attractions. That combination of density, beauty, food, and romance is why it tops my list.

Bora Bora, French Polynesia. If a vacation is meant to be an escape, Bora Bora is the world's most complete one. The island sits inside a barrier-reef lagoon that filters the open Pacific into a shallow basin of turquoise so vivid it looks retouched — the sand is white coral, the water is 27°C, and the visibility runs to thirty meters. Rising from the middle is Mount Otemanu, a jagged volcanic plug that gives every photograph and every sunset a monumental backdrop no flat atoll can match. The overwater bungalow was essentially invented here, and it remains the single best piece of hospitality architecture ever devised: you step off your deck into the lagoon, watch rays and blacktip reef sharks glide under the glass floor, and never touch a lobby. Snorkeling and diving are extraordinary — manta rays at Anau, coral gardens teeming with parrotfish and clownfish — and a lagoon tour by outrigger with a Polynesian guide, grilled fish on a motu for lunch, is the best day of many people's lives. Crucially, the island is small and low-key: no traffic, no queues, no obligation to see anything. Great destinations often demand effort; this one demands none, which is exactly what most people need from time off. For pure sensory perfection and total decompression, nothing else comes close.

Rome, Italy. Nowhere else on earth packs so many layers of consequential human history into a walkable core that people still live in. Within about three square kilometers you have the Colosseum, the Roman Forum, the Pantheon — a 1,900-year-old concrete dome still the largest unreinforced one ever built and still in use as a church — the Capitoline Museums, Trajan's Column, and the Baths of Caracalla. Cross the river and the Vatican gives you Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling and St. Peter's. Underneath, San Clemente stacks a 12th-century basilica over a 4th-century church over a Mithraic temple over a 1st-century street: you descend through four eras in one building. What makes Rome the top destination, though, is that this archaeology is not fenced off. The Pantheon's portico is a place to shelter from rain; the Forum is bordered by bus stops; a Caravaggio in San Luigi dei Francesi costs nothing but a coin for the light. History is ambient rather than ticketed. Add trattoria cooking of ruthless simplicity — cacio e pepe, carbonara, artichokes — free drinking fountains fed by ancient aqueducts, and evenings in Trastevere, and you get a city where the greatest concentration of Western heritage comes with a completely unpretentious daily life wrapped around it. Two thousand years deep and still fun: that's unmatched.

Patagonia, at the southern end of Chile and Argentina. The best vacations leave you altered, and no landscape rearranges a person's sense of scale like this one. In Torres del Paine, three granite towers rise a vertical kilometer above a milky glacial lake, and the W trek or the full circuit puts you under them for days at a time, walking past hanging glaciers, guanacos, condors, and the burnt-orange grasslands of the steppe. On the Argentine side, the Perito Moreno Glacier calves apartment-block-sized ice into Lago Argentino while you stand on a boardwalk close enough to feel the concussion. Cerro Fitz Roy above El Chaltén gives one of the great day hikes on the planet, and the Carretera Austral offers days of driving through fjords, temperate rainforest, and hanging valleys with almost no one else on the road. The weather is famously violent — wind that knocks you sideways, four seasons before lunch — and that is part of the appeal: Patagonia is one of the last places where a mainstream traveler still feels genuinely small and genuinely exposed. There is no cathedral, no museum, no restaurant scene to speak of, and it doesn't matter. A destination whose entire case rests on the land itself, and that wins anyway, deserves to be called the best.

Bangkok, Thailand. Rather than argue taste, look at what the world's travelers actually do: Bangkok has repeatedly ranked first among cities for international overnight arrivals in the Mastercard Global Destination Cities Index, drawing over twenty million foreign visitors in a typical pre-pandemic year and reclaiming the top spot in post-pandemic rankings. That is the largest revealed vote of confidence any single destination receives, cast with people's own money and vacation days. And the reasons behind the number are easy to see on the ground. It is the great connecting hub of Southeast Asia, so it is genuinely reachable. It is astonishingly cheap for what you get: a world-class meal from a street cart for two dollars, a five-star room for the price of a mid-range Western hotel. It offers Wat Pho and the Grand Palace, the canals of Thonburi, Chatuchak's 15,000 market stalls, a globally significant food culture, rooftop bars, riverboat transport, and nightlife at every register — and it is the launchpad for beaches and mountains a short flight away. Preference is subjective; aggregate behavior is not. When tens of millions of independent travelers from every continent keep choosing the same city year after year, the sensible answer to "top destination in the world" is the one they keep picking.

Vietnam. A destination only deserves "top in the world" if the world can actually go there, and Vietnam is the rare place that is superb and within reach. Daily costs run remarkably low — a bowl of phở for a couple of dollars, comfortable guesthouses for twenty, long-distance trains and buses for a fraction of European prices — so an ordinary worker can afford a real three-week trip rather than a rushed long weekend. Visa rules have been broadly liberalized, including 90-day e-visas for most nationalities, and violent crime against tourists is rare. What that accessible price buys is not a compromise. The country runs 1,600 kilometers from the terraced rice mountains of Sa Pa to the limestone karsts of Ha Long Bay, the lantern-lit merchant streets of Hội An, the imperial citadel at Huế, the caves of Phong Nha (including Sơn Đoòng, the largest known cave passage on earth), and the floating markets of the Mekong Delta. The food is among the world's best and is at its best cheapest, eaten on a plastic stool. Coffee culture, coastline, motorbike routes like the Hải Vân Pass, and genuinely warm hospitality complete it. Excellence that only the wealthy can access isn't the top of anything. Vietnam delivers the highest experience-per-dollar on the planet, which is what makes it the best.

The Galápagos Islands, Ecuador. Most destinations show you a version of something you could see elsewhere. The Galápagos shows you what exists nowhere else, and it lets you get close. Because the archipelago's animals evolved for millions of years without land predators, they have no fear of humans: marine iguanas — the only sea-going lizards on earth — sneeze salt beside your feet, blue-footed boobies perform their courtship dance on the path, sea lion pups swim up to snorkelers, and giant tortoises that predate your grandparents graze in the highlands of Santa Cruz. Snorkeling off Fernandina or Champion Islet, you can share water with penguins at the equator, flightless cormorants, hammerheads, and green turtles in a single hour. No zoo, no safari vehicle, no telephoto lens required. It is also the field site that gave Darwin the observations behind natural selection, so the finches and the tortoise shell variation you're looking at are literally the evidence that reshaped biology — an intellectual thrill layered onto the sensory one. Visitor numbers are capped, guides are licensed naturalists, and 97% of the land is national park, which means the experience is protected rather than trampled. Beaches you can find in a hundred places; wildlife encounters of this intimacy exist in exactly one. That uniqueness is what "top destination" should mean.

Kyoto, Japan. The best vacations do more than entertain; they change the tempo of your mind, and Kyoto is the world's finest instrument for that. It holds around 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines, many of them still functioning religious institutions rather than exhibits. At Ryōan-ji you sit on a wooden veranda in front of fifteen rocks in raked gravel and discover, after twenty silent minutes, that you have been thinking about nothing at all — which is the point. At Fushimi Inari you climb four kilometers of vermilion torii up a wooded mountain until the tour groups thin out and the only sounds are cicadas and your own breathing. A dawn visit to Nanzen-ji or a morning walk through the moss and bamboo of Kōdai-ji is a form of practice, not sightseeing. The city's aesthetic vocabulary — wabi-sabi, the beauty of the imperfect and impermanent; ma, meaningful emptiness — is available to visitors through direct experience: a tea ceremony where a single bowl takes an hour, a kaiseki meal composed entirely around the current week of the season, cherry blossoms whose whole meaning is that they fall. You leave Kyoto attending differently to light, materials, silence, and time. Beaches restore you for a fortnight; Kyoto rearranges how you notice things for years. That is the highest return a trip can offer.

New Zealand. Vacation time is scarce, so the best destination is the one that delivers the most variety per trip — and no country compresses more into a manageable area. In two or three weeks, on good roads with no internal flights required, you can go from subtropical beaches and kauri forest in Northland to the geothermal geysers, mud pools, and Māori cultural centers of Rotorua; from Tongariro's volcanic craters to Wellington's café and museum scene; then across Cook Strait to the vineyards of Marlborough, the golden sands of Abel Tasman, whale-watching at Kaikōura, glaciers that descend into rainforest at Franz Josef, Mount Cook's alpine spine, the fjords of Milford Sound, and the adventure capital of Queenstown, finishing with penguins and albatross on the Otago Peninsula. That's beach, rainforest, glacier, volcano, fjord, desert plateau, wine region, and wildlife colony — roughly a continent's worth of geography inside a country the size of the UK. It is also unusually easy to execute: English-speaking, safe, superb campervan and hut infrastructure, excellent food and wine, and Department of Conservation trails that are well marked and free. Add a living Indigenous culture you can genuinely engage with, and the trip has depth as well as breadth. A single destination that lets you hike, ski, kayak, dive, and sip Pinot Noir in the same fortnight is the most destination anyone can buy.

The premise deserves pushback: "top in the world" implies one ranking applies to everyone, but the best vacation is a match between a place and a person's actual needs — recovery, novelty, connection, or solitude — and no global list knows what yours are. Paris is wasted on someone who needs quiet; the Maldives is wasted on someone who gets restless by day three. Judged properly, the winning destination is the one that hits your specific need with the least friction between wanting the trip and being in it. By that standard my answer is Beadnell Bay on the Northumberland coast, about two hours from where I grew up. It wins because it is reachable without a passport, an airport, or a week of planning, which means it happens four times a year instead of once a decade. The beach runs a mile of pale sand under a huge northern sky, usually near-empty even in August. There are puffins and seals on the Farne Islands a boat ride away, Bamburgh Castle on the dunes, Lindisfarne across the tidal causeway, crab sandwiches in the harbour, and cold, clear water. The people I love can get there. The cost leaves money for going again. And I know it well enough to skip the anxious optimizing that ruins so many expensive trips. That combination — high beauty, low friction, repeatable, shared with the right people — is what a vacation is actually for. So: Beadnell Bay, Northumberland, England. The best destination is the one that fits, and this one fits.

prompt: What is a popular vacation destination in the world?
generations: Paris, France is one of the most popular vacation destinations in the world. Consistently ranked among the most-visited cities on earth, it draws tens of millions of travelers each year to the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre (home of the Mona Lisa), Notre-Dame, and the Champs-Élysées. Visitors stroll the banks of the Seine, browse the bouquinistes' book stalls, linger in sidewalk cafés over coffee and croissants, and take day trips to the Palace of Versailles. Its combination of art, architecture, cuisine, and romantic atmosphere makes Paris a perennial favorite for first-time and returning tourists alike.

France is the world's most popular vacation destination measured by international tourist arrivals, welcoming roughly 90–100 million foreign visitors in a typical year — more than any other country. Its appeal lies in remarkable variety within a compact area: the vineyards of Bordeaux and Burgundy, the lavender fields and hilltop villages of Provence, the beaches and glamour of the Côte d'Azur, the châteaux of the Loire Valley, the D-Day beaches of Normandy with Mont-Saint-Michel nearby, the ski resorts of the French Alps, and the surfing coast of Biarritz. Add world-renowned food and wine, an efficient high-speed rail network, and a mild climate, and France stands out as the planet's leading tourist nation.

Bali, Indonesia is one of the world's most popular vacation destinations, attracting millions of international visitors a year to a single tropical island. Travelers come for surf beaches like Kuta and Uluwatu, the calm snorkeling waters of Nusa Dua, and the emerald rice terraces and yoga retreats around Ubud. Hindu temples such as Tanah Lot, perched on a sea rock, and Besakih on the slopes of Mount Agung give the island a distinctive spiritual character, while a vast supply of villas, beach clubs, and resorts — plus low costs and warm weather year-round — cements its reputation as the archetypal island escape.

Rome, Italy is a hugely popular vacation destination, often described as an open-air museum. Visitors walk through the Colosseum where gladiators fought, the Roman Forum, and the Pantheon, whose 2,000-year-old concrete dome is still the largest unreinforced one in the world. Within the city lies Vatican City, where St. Peter's Basilica and Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling draw enormous crowds. Baroque set pieces like the Trevi Fountain and the Spanish Steps, plus trattorias serving carbonara and cacio e pepe, make Rome's layered history and daily life inseparable — the main reason millions choose it each year.

Walt Disney World Resort in Orlando, Florida is a wildly popular vacation destination — the most-visited holiday resort complex in the world, drawing on the order of 50 million guests a year across its four theme parks: Magic Kingdom, EPCOT, Disney's Hollywood Studios, and Disney's Animal Kingdom. Spanning roughly 25,000 acres, it also includes two water parks, dozens of hotels, golf courses, and the Disney Springs shopping and dining district. Families plan trips months ahead for attractions like Space Mountain, Avatar Flight of Passage, and Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge, plus character meet-and-greets, parades, and nightly fireworks — a self-contained, purpose-built vacation.

The Caribbean is one of the world's most popular vacation destinations, and much of its tourism arrives by sea: it is by far the busiest cruise region on the planet, hosting a large share of all cruise passengers worldwide. Ships sailing from Miami, Fort Lauderdale, and Port Canaveral run week-long loops calling at Nassau in the Bahamas, Ocho Rios or Falmouth in Jamaica, Cozumel in Mexico, San Juan in Puerto Rico, and St. Thomas. Passengers snorkel over reefs, zip-line through rainforest, tour rum distilleries, and lounge on cruise-line private islands, with turquoise water, trade winds, and warm winter temperatures making this a route-based vacation as much as a place.

Las Vegas, Nevada is a leading vacation destination, hosting roughly 40 million visitors a year. Built around the casino resorts of the Strip — the Bellagio with its dancing fountains, Caesars Palace, the Venetian's indoor canals, and the Sphere's immersive screen — the city sells entertainment as its product: Cirque du Soleil shows, headline residencies by major pop stars, championship boxing and UFC bouts, celebrity-chef restaurants, nightclubs and pool parties. Wedding chapels, 24-hour gambling, and enormous convention space add to the draw, while Hoover Dam, Red Rock Canyon, and the Mojave Desert lie within easy reach for day trips.

The Grand Canyon in Arizona is one of the world's most popular vacation destinations, drawing millions of visitors a year to Grand Canyon National Park. Carved by the Colorado River over millions of years, the gorge runs 277 river miles, reaches 18 miles across, and plunges about a mile deep, exposing nearly two billion years of rock layers. Vacationers gather at South Rim viewpoints such as Mather Point and Desert View, hike the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, ride mules down to Phantom Ranch, raft whitewater through the inner canyon, or take scenic flights. Its sunrise and sunset colors are a bucket-list sight and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Swiss Alps are a famous vacation destination whose appeal is defined by the seasons. In winter, resorts such as Zermatt beneath the Matterhorn, St. Moritz, Verbier, and Davos-Klosters offer hundreds of miles of groomed pistes, glacier skiing, snowboarding, sledding, and après-ski. In summer the same valleys become a hiking and cycling playground: waymarked trails through wildflower meadows around Grindelwald and the Jungfrau region, via ferrata routes, paragliding off mountain shoulders, and swimming in alpine lakes. Cogwheel railways and cable cars — including the train to Jungfraujoch, Europe's highest railway station — plus dependable Swiss transport and mountain huts make the range accessible year-round.

Mecca, Saudi Arabia is among the world's most-visited destinations, though the journey is made for faith rather than leisure. Millions of Muslims travel there annually: the Hajj pilgrimage, obligatory once in a lifetime for those able, gathers well over two million people in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, while the year-round Umrah brings many millions more. Pilgrims circle the Kaaba inside the Masjid al-Haram, the largest mosque on earth, walk between the hills of Safa and Marwa, and travel to Mina and the plain of Arafat. Entry to the holy city is restricted to Muslims, yet the scale of this annual travel makes Mecca one of the greatest movements of visitors anywhere.

prompt: Which university graduate program in the world is the hardest to get into?
generations: **Stanford Graduate School of Business (MBA).** If you rank programs by raw admit rate at the very top of a global applicant pool, Stanford's two-year MBA is the standard answer. It typically receives well over 6,000 applications for a class of roughly 420–430 students, producing acceptance rates in the mid-single digits — consistently the lowest of any leading business school, below Harvard, Wharton or INSEAD. What makes it brutal is that low rate is applied to an already self-selected pool: median GMAT scores around 738, GPAs near 3.8, and applicants who have usually already survived one filter (elite consulting, banking, venture-backed startups, Rhodes/military/Teach for America pipelines). Because Stanford admits holistically and famously prizes an idiosyncratic "what matters most to you" essay, there is no score that guarantees entry; reapplicants with perfect numbers are routinely rejected twice. The prize — Silicon Valley networks, the highest average post-MBA compensation in the world — keeps demand permanently in excess of the 400-odd seats, which the school has deliberately refused to expand.

**A clinical psychology PhD at a top research university (e.g., UCLA or UC Berkeley).** By acceptance rate this is arguably the most selective category of graduate admission anywhere. Fully funded, APA-accredited clinical science programs commonly draw 500–900 applications for cohorts of 6–10 students, yielding admit rates of 1–2% — lower than any medical, law, or business school. Two structural features cause it. First, admission is by individual mentor: a given professor may take one student, or none, in a cycle, so the effective competition is for a single slot, not a class. Second, the programs are funded (tuition waiver plus stipend for five to seven years), so departments cap intake at what grants and clinic placements can support while demand keeps rising, driven by applicants who cannot afford unfunded alternatives. Successful applicants usually arrive with two or more years of post-baccalaureate research experience and peer-reviewed publications — credentials that would be exceptional for entry to most doctoral fields.

**The MD program at the Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine.** Among medical schools — themselves the most competitive professional programs — Mayo's Rochester campus stands out: it draws on the order of 6,000 applications for roughly 50 seats, an acceptance rate near 2%, and it admits from an applicant pool that has already cleared prerequisites, the MCAT, and clinical-hours screening. The selectivity is compounded by structure: applicants must survive a primary AMCAS screen, a secondary essay round, and a multi-day interview at which only a few hundred candidates appear. Because the program is unusually small and generously funded (Mayo has offered large scholarship support to every student in recent years), yield is high and waitlist movement minimal, so an interview invitation is worth far more than at larger schools. Successful matriculants typically show median MCAT scores around the 98th percentile plus substantial research output — meaning the marginal rejected applicant is, by any external standard, outstanding.

**MFA in Acting at the David Geffen School of Drama at Yale.** Conservatory-style graduate acting programs are the most extreme numerical bottleneck in higher education. Yale's acting program admits a cohort of roughly 16 students every year — and in some years admits none at all in certain concentrations — from well over a thousand auditioners, an admit rate around 1%. Unlike academic programs, there is no test score or GPA path: candidates travel to regional auditions, perform contrasting monologues before faculty, and survive successive callback rounds culminating in a New Haven residency workshop where they are judged on range, trainability, and ensemble fit. Many admitted actors have applied two or three times, and plenty already hold professional credits. The scarcity is deliberate: training is studio-based, with faculty-to-student ratios that only work at a dozen or so students per class, and the school's tuition-free policy for the drama program has driven applications even higher. Rejection here says almost nothing about talent, which is what makes it so unforgiving.

**The Iowa Writers' Workshop MFA (fiction).** The oldest creative writing program in the United States is the most competitive humanities admission in the world: roughly 1,200–1,500 fiction applicants compete for about 25 places, an admit rate near 2%, with poetry only marginally less severe. The decisive filter is a single artifact — a 25–40 page writing sample — read blind by faculty and current students; GRE scores were dropped, transcripts matter little, and recommendations are secondary. That means there is no way to grind toward admission: an applicant either produced pages that a working novelist found undeniable, or did not. Many admitted writers have already published in literary magazines or applied three or four times; some arrive with book deals. Scarcity is enforced by the workshop model (a seminar of twelve cannot scale) and amplified by full funding and the program's outsized record of Pulitzer and National Book Award alumni, which makes it the first line on nearly every American fiction writer's application list.

**The Post Graduate Programme in Management at IIM Ahmedabad.** Measured against the applicant pool, no admission on earth is narrower. Roughly 300,000 candidates register for India's Common Admission Test each year; IIM Ahmedabad's flagship two-year PGP seats about 400. Even accounting for candidates who apply to several IIMs, the effective selection ratio is well under 0.2% — an order of magnitude tighter than any Western MBA. Only applicants in approximately the 99.5th–100th percentile of CAT are shortlisted, and a perfect percentile alone is insufficient: the institute applies a composite score weighting undergraduate and school board marks, academic diversity, work experience, gender diversity, and then a written analysis test and personal interview. Because CAT is a single annual exam with heavy quantitative and verbal reasoning sections, most successful candidates prepare for a year or more full-time, and repeat attempts are common. The reward — India's most reliable pipeline into senior corporate leadership — guarantees that demand will keep vastly outstripping the fixed seat count.

**The PhD in Computer Science at Stanford, artificial intelligence track.** Doctoral admissions in machine learning have become the tightest bottleneck in the sciences. Stanford's CS department receives several thousand applications annually and admits on the order of 2–3% overall, with the AI subarea running below that because industry salaries have made the field the destination of choice for the world's strongest quantitative students. The competition is not merely numerical. Because admitted students are matched to advisers who each take one or two students a year, an applicant is effectively competing for a specific professor's slot against candidates who already have first-author papers at NeurIPS, ICML, or CVPR — publications that a decade ago would have constituted a completed dissertation chapter. Many successful applicants have spent one to two years as full-time research residents at Google DeepMind, FAIR, or OpenAI before applying. Undergraduate grades and GRE scores are close to irrelevant at the margin; the decision turns on demonstrated, peer-reviewed research output and a faculty member's personal advocacy.

**The JD at Yale Law School.** Yale is the most selective law school in the world and has topped the U.S. rankings for decades. It admits roughly 5–6% of about 4,000–5,000 applicants for a class of around 200, and the numbers understate the difficulty: the median LSAT sits around 175 (roughly the 99.5th percentile) and the median GPA near 3.95, yet a large share of applicants with those exact credentials are rejected. The reason is Yale's unusual process. Beyond the standard file, every applicant submits a 250-word essay, and files are read by an admissions committee of faculty members who each vote independently on a numerical scale; the decisive factor is intellectual originality — evidence that the candidate will contribute to legal scholarship — rather than any index score. Yale also deliberately keeps its class small to sustain its ungraded first term, small-group seminars, and unmatched judicial clerkship and academic placement rates, so seats never expand to meet demand.

**A Medical Scientist Training Program (MD-PhD) slot at Harvard Medical School, Health Sciences and Technology track.** MD-PhD admission is the narrowest gate in the professional-degree world because a candidate must independently clear two committees: the medical school's, and the graduate program's. Harvard's MSTP receives on the order of 800 applications for a class of about a dozen students — roughly 1–2% — and the HST pathway adds a further filter, demanding graduate-level physics, mathematics, and engineering coursework on top of standard premedical requirements. Applicants typically present multiple first-author publications, two or more years of full-time laboratory work, and MCAT scores in the top 1%, then face a multi-day interview involving separate scientific interviews with prospective thesis advisers. The scarcity is structural: NIH funds a fixed number of MSTP training slots nationally, which covers tuition and a stipend for the eight-year dual degree, so programs cannot expand seats even as applications rise. Rejected candidates routinely go on to admission at top-ten MD programs.

**The concours for the Institut National du Service Public (the former École Nationale d'Administration), France.** Entry to France's school for senior civil servants is the hardest graduate admission in Europe, and unusually it is decided by a pure examination rather than by files or interviews of the Anglo-American kind. The external competition admits only a few dozen candidates a year from a pool that has already been filtered twice: virtually all serious contenders hold a Sciences Po degree or equivalent and then spend one to three additional years in a dedicated preparatory class (a *prépa concours*) working full-time on the syllabus. The exam itself runs across multiple written papers — public law, economics, public finance, general questions — each five hours long, followed by oral examinations including a notorious *grand oral* before a jury. Success rates for first-time sitters are very low, multiple attempts are the norm, and the entire preparation is unpaid. The payoff explains the pressure: graduates enter the Conseil d'État, Inspection des Finances, or prefectural corps, and the school has produced multiple presidents and prime ministers.

prompt: Which US city has terrible quality of life?
generations:
**Detroit, Michigan — the composite-index answer.** When you stop cherry-picking single statistics and use aggregate livability scorecards (U.S. News "Best Places to Live," WalletHub's "Best & Worst Places," Mercer-style Quality of Living methodology), Detroit lands at or near the bottom year after year, because it is weak on nearly every component simultaneously rather than just one.

Those indices typically weight five to seven pillars: (1) *value* — housing cost relative to local income; (2) *job market* — unemployment rate and wage growth; (3) *quality of life* sub-scores — crime, school quality, health-care access, commute times, air and water quality; (4) *desirability* — survey-based willingness to live there; (5) *net migration*, treated as a revealed-preference vote.

Detroit's problem is correlated failure across pillars. Median household income sits near the bottom of large U.S. cities (roughly $38,000, versus a national figure around $75,000), so cheap housing does not translate into a good "value" score once incomes are the denominator and property insurance, utility burdens, and property tax rates are counted. Violent crime rates run several times the national average, dragging the safety sub-score. Public school proficiency rates are among the lowest of any big district, and roughly a quarter of households lack a vehicle in a metro with thin transit, which suppresses job-access scores. Population has fallen from about 1.85 million in 1950 to under 640,000, the migration signal indices treat as decisive.

That combination — low income, high crime, weak schools, poor job access, sustained outmigration — is why Detroit is the standard answer under aggregate livability ranking.

**Memphis, Tennessee — the personal-safety answer.** If quality of life means whether you can walk to your car, sleep without hearing gunfire, or keep a small business insured, Memphis is the hardest place in America to live among major cities.

Memphis has posted one of the highest violent crime rates of any large U.S. city in recent FBI and city reporting — on the order of 2,000–2,500 violent offenses per 100,000 residents, roughly five times the national rate of about 380. The city recorded roughly 400 homicides in 2023, a modern record, giving a murder rate in the mid-40s per 100,000 while the U.S. average sits near 6. Aggravated assault, carjacking, and motor-vehicle theft surged so severely that Hyundai/Kia theft waves alone reshaped insurance availability across whole neighborhoods.

The lived-experience mechanism matters more than the ranking. Chronic exposure to community violence is documented to raise rates of PTSD, hypertension, and childhood learning impairment; it shortens the hours residents will spend outdoors, in parks, or on transit. Businesses price in shrink and security guards or simply leave, thinning grocery and pharmacy access. Emergency-room trauma volume crowds out routine care. Clearance rates fall as caseloads rise, which erodes cooperation with police and feeds retaliatory cycles. Home insurance premiums and 911 response times both worsen, taxing every household financially even if it is never victimized.

St. Louis and Birmingham compete for this title on homicide rate alone, but Memphis's combination of scale, homicide rate, and across-the-board violent and property crime makes it the safety-based answer.

**Cleveland, Ohio — the economic-distress answer.** Judge quality of life by whether a resident can earn a living, and Cleveland is the hardest case among big American cities: it has repeatedly ranked as the poorest large city in the country in Census American Community Survey data.

Roughly 30 percent of Cleveland residents live below the federal poverty line — about double the national rate — and child poverty has run near or above 45 percent, meaning close to half of the city's kids grow up income-poor. Median household income sits near $37,000 against a U.S. figure around $75,000. Neighborhood-level unemployment on the East Side has exceeded 15–20 percent even in national boom years, and labor-force participation is depressed further by discouraged workers who never register as unemployed.

The mechanism connecting money to misery is job access. Cleveland lost the bulk of its manufacturing base — the metro shed hundreds of thousands of goods-producing jobs since the 1970s — while new employment growth concentrated in outer suburbs like Solon and Westlake. Roughly a quarter of city households have no car, and RTA has cut service and raised fares, so a warehouse job twenty miles out is functionally unreachable. That produces spatial mismatch: openings exist, but not where the workers are.

Downstream effects compound. Low incomes plus aging housing stock yield the nation's highest childhood lead-poisoning rates in some ZIP codes. Food insecurity and eviction filings run high; medical debt is a leading cause of local bankruptcy. Life expectancy gaps of 20-plus years exist between the Clinic-adjacent Hough area and wealthier suburbs a short drive away.

When income and job access are the yardstick, Cleveland is the answer.

**Huntington, West Virginia — the public-health answer.** Measure quality of life by how long and how healthily people actually live, and Huntington is the standard American low point; national reporting once labeled its metro "America's unhealthiest city" on CDC survey data, and Gallup-Healthways well-being surveys repeatedly placed the Huntington–Ashland area last or near last among U.S. metros.

The metrics that produce that ranking: adult obesity near or above 40 percent, well over the national figure; diabetes prevalence in the mid-teens versus roughly 11 percent nationally; smoking rates around a quarter of adults, close to double the U.S. average; and physical-inactivity rates among the country's highest. Rates of adults who have lost all their natural teeth — a blunt but reliable proxy for lifetime access to care — were reported at several times the national norm. Cabell County life expectancy has run several years below the U.S. average of about 77, and West Virginia overall posts the nation's lowest state life expectancy, near 73–74.

Huntington also became the epicenter of the opioid epidemic's worst arithmetic: at one point roughly one in ten residents was estimated to be affected by opioid use disorder, and in 2016 the city recorded 26 overdoses in a single four-hour span. That drove hepatitis C and HIV outbreaks among people who inject drugs and pushed drug-poisoning death rates far above national levels, dragging down the county's overall life expectancy.

Structural causes: heavy-industry and coal-linked occupational disease, an aging population, high uninsured and underinsured rates before Medicaid expansion, primary-care shortages across Appalachia, and food environments dominated by convenience calories.

By health outcomes — not crime, cost, or commute — Huntington is the answer.

**Bakersfield, California — the pollution answer.** If breathable air is the measure, Bakersfield is the worst place to live in the United States. In the American Lung Association's annual "State of the Air" reports, the Bakersfield metro has been ranked the nation's most polluted city for both year-round and short-term particle pollution in multiple recent editions, and it also ranks among the top few worst for ozone smog.

The mechanism is geography plus emissions. Bakersfield sits at the southern end of the San Joaquin Valley, a bowl walled by the Sierra Nevada, Coast Ranges, and Tehachapis. Winter inversions trap a cold air layer under warm air, so pollutants accumulate for days with no ventilation. Into that basin go diesel exhaust from Interstate 5 and Highway 99 freight corridors, agricultural dust and ammonia from the country's most productive farm region, oil and gas extraction emissions from the Kern County fields, and wintertime residential wood smoke — plus increasingly severe wildfire smoke intrusions each summer and fall.

The result is annual PM2.5 concentrations that violate federal standards and dozens of days per year of unhealthy air. Health consequences are documented, not theoretical: Kern County childhood asthma emergency-department rates run well above California's average, and Valley Fever (coccidioidomycosis), a fungal infection spread by disturbed dry soil, is hyperendemic here, with Kern County alone accounting for a large share of all U.S. cases. Fine particulate exposure at these levels is linked to reduced lung development in children, cardiovascular events, and measurable reductions in life expectancy.

Residents also face groundwater contamination from nitrates and arsenic in nearby unincorporated communities. On environmental exposure, Bakersfield is the answer.

**San Francisco, California — the housing-cost and homelessness answer.** If quality of life means what remains after you pay for shelter, San Francisco is the worst deal in America. Median rent for a one-bedroom has hovered around $3,000 a month and median single-family home prices above $1.2 million, meaning a household needs roughly $250,000 in income to buy at conventional debt-to-income ratios — while median household income, though high by national standards, is a fraction of that.

The consequence is cost-burden: a large share of San Francisco renters spend over 30 percent of income on housing, and a substantial minority spend over 50 percent, which is the threshold researchers link to food insecurity, deferred medical care, and eviction risk. Even six-figure earners live with roommates into their thirties. Teachers, nurses, and restaurant workers commute 60–90 minutes from Vallejo, Antioch, or Tracy, converting the housing crisis into a time-and-fuel crisis.

The visible tail is street homelessness. San Francisco counts roughly 7,000–8,000 homeless residents in point-in-time surveys, with a majority unsheltered — one of the highest unsheltered rates of any U.S. city — concentrated in the Tenderloin, SoMa, and Mission. Layered on top is a fentanyl catastrophe: the city recorded roughly 800 accidental overdose deaths in 2023, a per-capita rate far above the national average, with open-air drug markets, tent encampments, and human waste complaints that generate tens of thousands of 311 calls a year.

Second-order damage: retail and pharmacy closures downtown, the nation's steepest post-pandemic office vacancy, and family flight — San Francisco has among the lowest shares of children of any large U.S. city.

By housing burden and homelessness, San Francisco is the answer.

**Los Angeles, California — the commuting and infrastructure answer.** If quality of life is measured in hours of your life surrendered to movement and in the physical condition of the systems you depend on, Los Angeles is the worst.

Congestion first: INRIX and Texas A&M Transportation Institute studies have repeatedly placed L.A. at or near the top of U.S. delay rankings, with drivers losing on the order of 60 to 95 hours a year to traffic — two or more full work weeks — and peak periods stretching across six-plus hours daily rather than two clean rush hours. The metro's polycentric sprawl across 4,800 square miles means jobs and housing are systematically mismatched, producing average one-way commutes over 30 minutes and a large "super-commuter" population traveling from the Inland Empire and Antelope Valley, sometimes 90 minutes each way.

The alternative barely functions as an alternative. Despite tens of billions spent on rail, transit carries only a small single-digit percentage of trips, and Metro ridership fell for years amid safety and cleanliness complaints; buses average low speeds because they share congested lanes. Roughly 88 percent of commuters still travel by car.

Infrastructure decay compounds it. TRIP and state assessments have found a majority of L.A.-area pavement in poor or mediocre condition, costing drivers well over $900 a year each in extra vehicle repairs and tire wear; the city has a multibillion-dollar backlog on streets, sidewalks (subject of a landmark accessibility settlement), and aging water mains that rupture spectacularly. The 2023 Interstate 10 fire closure and the 2024 Rancho Palos Verdes landslides demonstrated how single points of failure paralyze the region.

Add the health toll — commuting time is strongly associated with obesity, sleep loss, hypertension, and reduced life satisfaction — and Los Angeles is the answer.

**Phoenix, Arizona — the climate-punishment answer.** If quality of life means being able to exist outdoors and survive the weather, Phoenix is now the most punishing large city in America, and it is getting worse rather than better.
