"Half full" congratulates you on the status quo. This isn't gloom; it's the ordinary discipline of anyone who maintains anything. Pilots read fuel remaining. Nurses chart what the patient still can't do. Engineers list open defects, not closed ones. None of them are depressed — they're accurate, and their accuracy is what keeps the glass from reaching empty at all. Optimism about a half-empty glass is fine, but it has to come after the measurement, not instead of it. So I'll name the gap first: half empty.

Half full — because of where I'm standing, and I'd give a different answer standing somewhere else. The right frame isn't a personality trait, it's a function of your role and what your errors cost. Put me in the auditor's chair, the anesthesiologist's, the structural reviewer's, and I say half empty without hesitation: those jobs are defined by catching the missing piece, and a cheerful reading of an incomplete checklist is professional negligence. Their asymmetry runs one way — a false reassurance kills, a false alarm costs an hour. But my actual seat here is the other kind. I'm in the position of the coach, the founder, the person trying to get a tired team to attempt one more thing. In that seat the scarce input isn't information about the gap; everyone already knows the gap, they can see it, they talk about it at lunch. The scarce input is the belief that the remaining half is gettable. Announcing the emptiness there doesn't add data, it subtracts willingness. So the honest answer is role-indexed, and my role indexes to half full. Ask me again when I'm signing off on someone's blueprints.

Half full — because a glass with water in it has a history, and history is the only thing that makes the phrase mean anything. Water does not appear in glasses spontaneously. Every half-filled glass on a table got there by someone pouring, which is to say by a process running from zero toward the brim. Read as a snapshot, "half full" and "half empty" are indistinguishable; read as a frame of a film, they differ in the direction of the arrow. "Half empty" properly describes a glass mid-drain: the one being drunk from, the one leaking, the tank running down toward zero. "Half full" describes a glass mid-fill. Given no other information, the base rate favors filling — glasses are filled deliberately and often, and are usually emptied all the way in one sitting, so a glass caught at the midpoint is more likely on its way up than paused on its way down. That's an empirical claim about kettles, pitchers, and taps, not an attitude. So I pick half full on the trajectory, and I'd switch the instant I saw a straw in it.

Half empty. In any system that actually handles liquid, the quantity you specify, monitor, and pay for is the space that is not liquid — the ullage, the headspace, the freeboard. A tanker is loaded to leave room for thermal expansion; a bottle of beer needs headspace for the carbonation to sit in; a fermenter that is topped up foams over; a fuel bladder is filled to a percentage precisely so the vapor volume stays within limits. The liquid volume is bookkeeping. The empty volume is engineering. It's also the answer to the only practical question anyone asks at a table, which is "can you top that up?" — and the answer to that is a headspace figure, not a contents figure. Pouring, mixing, stirring without slopping, carrying without spilling, chilling a drink with ice: every one of those operations consumes the empty half and is limited by it. So the operationally meaningful reading of a glass at the midpoint is that it has 50% remaining capacity available. Half empty, and the emptiness is the specification.

Half full — because what is actually present is the only thing I have any business calling real. The water is here, in the glass, now. The absent half is a comparison I invented by imagining a fuller glass that does not exist, and then grieving the difference. That's not observation; it's a small act of self-inflicted poverty. Practiced attention runs the other direction: notice the water, notice the glass, notice the hand holding it, notice that someone drew it and carried it and it is clean. Gratitude here isn't a wager on the future — I'm not predicting the glass will fill, and I'm not claiming things trend upward. It is simply an accurate inventory of what has been given. And the glass will not stay this way regardless. The water will be drunk, or it will evaporate, or the glass will break, and so will the hand and the table; everything at the midpoint is passing through. Knowing that, the appropriate response to half a glass is not accounting for the shortfall but drinking it with attention while it's here. Half full — a description of the given, not a forecast.

Half full — because that's what the language itself defaults to, and I see no reason to fight my own grammar. English scalar adjective pairs have an unmarked member, the one that names the dimension rather than a deviation from it. We ask "how long is the rope?" for ropes of every length, "how tall is she?" of children, "how old are you?" of babies. "How short is it?" already presupposes shortness. Full/empty behaves the same way: "how full is the glass?" is the neutral question you can ask of any glass, including an empty one, whereas "how empty is it?" is marked and drags in a presupposition — that emptiness is at issue, that the glass was fuller before, that something has been lost. Note also which term gives us the neutral quantity word: capacity is measured in what a vessel holds when full; there's no unit of emptiness. So the default, presupposition-free description of a glass at its midpoint is fifty percent of the way along the fullness scale. Half full isn't optimism; it's just the unmarked pole doing its ordinary job. Picking "half empty" would smuggle in a claim I haven't been given evidence for.

Half empty. I pick it because the choice is a test of frame-resistance, and the frames on offer are not politically neutral. Logically equivalent descriptions reliably move people's judgments — the same treatment described as "90% survive" versus "10% die" produces different consent — and everyone who wants something from you knows this. Which means the positive framing is the one you will be handed: by the vendor whose product is half built, by the manager whose project is half staffed, by the government whose program half works. "Half full" is the house frame. It arrives free, it flatters, and it counsels you to stop asking. Choosing "half empty" is therefore not gloom but hygiene: deliberately adopting the description that a salesman would never volunteer, because that's the description under which the shortfall stays visible and gets a name, a size, and an owner. Say "we've achieved half" and the meeting ends in applause; say "half of it is missing" and someone has to explain the missing half. I'd rather sit in the second meeting. Pick the frame that resists the spin: half empty.

Half full — as the less inaccurate of two bad options, because strictly speaking the glass is entirely full. There is no vacuum in your kitchen. Above the water sits a column of air, roughly 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen at about 101 kilopascals, containing on the order of 10^22 molecules in an ordinary tumbler's headspace — molecules with mass, pressure, and enough push to hold the water down. The glass therefore contains no empty region whatsoever; it contains two fluids of very different density, and the interface happens to sit at the midpoint. "Half empty" asserts that half the interior volume contains nothing, which is false as a matter of physics. "Half full" at least makes a true claim about the volume it names: half the glass is full of the liquid under discussion, and it says nothing false about the rest — it merely omits the air, which conversational shorthand is entitled to do. Given a forced choice between a statement that is false and a statement that is true but incomplete, I'll take true and incomplete. Half full, on the grounds of the nitrogen.

Half full — chosen by coin flip, tails, and I want the method on the record because the method is the whole point. The two phrases pick out identical states of the world; they are logically equivalent descriptions of one water line. So a preference between them cannot be evidence about how I handle adversity, whether I'm pleasant to work with, or what I expect from next year. It's evidence about which word came to mind first, which depends mostly on what the person asking said last and what I heard on a podcast. The premise of the question is that a snap lexical choice indexes a stable trait — and that premise is what I'm rejecting, not the glass. Real dispositions show up in behavior under cost: whether you make the second attempt, whether you check the thing you'd rather not check, whether you tell someone bad news early. None of that is predicted by a vibe about drinkware, and treating the answer as diagnostic mostly just tells people which answer to perform. So: half full, per the coin. Ask me something with a wrong answer if you want to learn anything about me.
